use_cases.summary:
I measured what agents on this repository actually look up, using scripts that run only on this machine over 1,452 transcripts (28,229 model calls). I split the work into two classes. Product-code work is 109 transcripts, all from 2026-11-13, with 3,124 lookup calls and 1,069 episodes. Program and document work is 1,343 transcripts, with 19,024 lookup calls and 3,763 episodes. Each lookup's cost is taken in three ways: tokens fetched (result characters divided by 2.42, a ratio measured from 4,938 context deltas), tokens carried (fetched tokens times the number of later calls in the same window), and the window re-read by the lookup step itself. Every call was given a plain-words question form by rule. A manual check found the rule right on about 3 calls in 4 (31-32 of 40 product, 22-24 of 30 program).

Findings:
- **Product work spends little on relations.** Of 242M carried tokens, 23% of all product context, the split is:
  - orientation and definition reads of code: 38%
  - documents (the phase assignment, design notes, defect registers, invariants, runbooks): 18%
  - relational questions (uses, contracts, tests, change sets, history, data model): 20%
  - non-graph reads (logs, run output, instructions): 24%
- **The session start is the single largest cost.** In 13 main product sessions, the lookups made before the first code edit cause 55% of carried lookup tokens (86M of 157M) and 47% of fetched tokens. They re-read the same plan sections, design notes (46 transcripts) and gate-document defect IDs (40 transcripts).
- **Program work is mostly documents.** Prior-lane findings take 45% of 1,147M carried tokens (the noisiest label), plan and design sections 16%, rules 6%.
- **Agents rarely fail to find things.** About 0.4-0.5% of searches come back empty, and about 2-3% of reads repeat the same range in the same window. What costs tokens is volume: about 5,000 tokens per orientation read, carried by 100-160 later calls.
- **Agents batch their lookups.** 86% of product lookups are shell commands, and 61% of those chain 2 or more lookups in one call.
- **v1 was tested on a minor case.** Its co-change target matches the question "what changed here recently", which is 1.8% of product carried tokens.

The notes file covers all of this in detail:
- 16 ranked competency questions, each with the nodes, relations and properties it needs
- what is not a graph question
- 7 corrections to the earlier rounds
- 5 recommendations, each with a test that could show it does not help (no installs needed)
- what could not be measured

competency_questions.question_form: CQ1 What did an earlier lane, round, agent or review conclude about X, and does it still hold?
competency_questions.example: Read the earlier round's bench log and notes; print the reviewer's report for PR N; read evidence files of a previous workflow lane
competency_questions.how_often: Program 6,332 calls in 2,210 episodes and 906 transcripts (noisiest label: includes some reads of the agent's own scratch files); product 8 calls
competency_questions.tokens_it_cost: Program 20.7M fetched, 521M carried (45% of program carried); about 1,282 exact cross-session duplicate reads (7.2M fetched tokens); product 0.9M carried
competency_questions.what_the_agent_did: cat, sed or Read of whole evidence and notes files, often in chunks, and greps for the item it needed; about 60% of these reads are never named again (weak proxy)
competency_questions.what_a_graph_would_need: Conclusion layer: claim, evidence and source nodes with author, date and strength; supports, refutes, supersedes and rests_on edges to code spans, document sections and commits; a validity property computed from the content hashes of what the claim rests on (the K0 dependency record)

competency_questions.question_form: CQ2 What does the plan or design say about my assignment: which phase, which findings, which decisions?
competency_questions.example: Print plan lines 24-115 and 1557-1793; grep the gate document for eleven defect IDs in one regular expression; print the area's design note in full
competency_questions.how_often: Product 245 calls in 139 episodes and 51 transcripts (design notes read in 46 product transcripts, gate defect IDs in 40); program 1,802 calls in 884 episodes
competency_questions.tokens_it_cost: Product 407k fetched, 20.4M carried, mostly at session start; program 8.6M fetched, 182M carried (16%)
competency_questions.what_the_agent_did: Fixed line ranges with sed or awk, full cat of design notes, and ID greps, repeated identically by each phase session before its first edit
competency_questions.what_a_graph_would_need: Nodes for phase, finding (register ID), decision or ruling (date), and document section (heading path, line span, hash); edges covers, described_in, anchored_at (code span) and supersedes; valid-from and valid-to on decisions

competency_questions.question_form: CQ3 How does subsystem S work now: which files, entry points, state and flows make it up?
competency_questions.example: Print the attendance queue, sync and punch modules in full; print the outbox, its sync module, the classification module and the API client
competency_questions.how_often: Product 173 calls in 81 episodes and 53 transcripts; program 304 calls
competency_questions.tokens_it_cost: Product 877k fetched, 50.0M carried (20.7%, the largest product form), about 5,069 tokens per call; program 45.4M carried
competency_questions.what_the_agent_did: cat -n of 3 to 10 whole files per call, mostly before the first edit; 55% of these reads are never named again (weak proxy)
competency_questions.what_a_graph_would_need: Nodes for slice (feature folder per runtime), file, symbol (kind, signature, first doc line, span), entry point (route, screen, scheduler job, background task), queue and storage key; edges contains, defines, imports, calls, reads_key, writes_key and enqueues; the answer is a card plus exact spans. Only partly a graph question: the bodies still have to be read

competency_questions.question_form: CQ4 Which rule (invariant, open defect, runbook step) constrains the code I am changing, and why?
competency_questions.example: Print invariants-file lines for the outbox rules; print open-work handoff sections by line range; grep the self-host runbook for schema statements
competency_questions.how_often: Product 277 calls in 127 episodes and 56 transcripts (invariants file in 22 transcripts, handoff in 22); program 1,143 calls
competency_questions.tokens_it_cost: Product 714k fetched, 21.0M carried (8.7%); program 3.1M fetched, 72.0M carried
competency_questions.what_the_agent_did: Section-range reads of the invariants file, the handoff and the runbooks, plus keyword greps
competency_questions.what_a_graph_would_need: Rule nodes (id, text span, hash, rationale); constrains edges to symbols, tables, settings, routes and outbox kinds; justified_by edges to defects and PRs; pushed as a warning when an edit touches a constrained node

competency_questions.question_form: CQ5 Where is X defined, with what signature, and what does its body say?
competency_questions.example: List every function and error raise in the jobs service, then print lines 726-1520; show the completion-mapping function with 22 lines after; find each queue's size-cap constant
competency_questions.how_often: Product 619 calls in 303 episodes and 76 transcripts; program 951 calls
competency_questions.tokens_it_cost: Product 789k fetched, 37.7M carried (15.6%), 88.1M lookup-step context (many small steps); program 37.5M carried
competency_questions.what_the_agent_did: grep -n for definition patterns with -A N, then sed -n line ranges; 20 same-window re-reads
competency_questions.what_a_graph_would_need: A symbol index (name and aliases to kind, file, span, signature) is enough; a graph adds nothing for the lookup itself

competency_questions.question_form: CQ6 What does this change set change, and what outside it depends on what it changed?
competency_questions.example: Diff base..head for the backend and one test; show a file as of a commit; then grep for users of the changed functions
competency_questions.how_often: Product 165 calls in 87 episodes and 33 transcripts (reviewers); program 306 calls
competency_questions.what_the_agent_did: git diff and git show sha:path, followed by git grep for users
competency_questions.what_a_graph_would_need: Two snapshots, or a version property on nodes and edges; a symbol-level diff; then reverse reachability (CQ8) and contract edges (CQ13) over the changed symbols. The diff text itself is not a graph question

competency_questions.question_form: CQ7 Which tests and fixtures exercise X, and how are similar tests set up?
competency_questions.example: How do existing integration tests set up an unassigned carry-in job and post a payment; print the conftest fixtures
competency_questions.how_often: Product 154 calls in 122 episodes and 32 transcripts; program 102 calls
competency_questions.what_the_agent_did: Read or grep test files and conftest for fixture names and request calls
competency_questions.what_a_graph_would_need: Nodes for test, fixture and seed; edges test_calls (symbol), test_requests (route) and uses_fixture

competency_questions.question_form: CQ8 Who uses, calls or references X, including by string literal; what breaks if it changes?
competency_questions.example: Where is the 'current status' message string used in both clients; every call of the enqueue function outside tests; every storage-key literal in the mobile app
competency_questions.how_often: Product 210 calls in 126 episodes and 64 transcripts; program 437 calls
competency_questions.what_the_agent_did: grep -rn or git grep across the runtimes with test files excluded; 60% of results never named again (weak proxy)
competency_questions.what_a_graph_would_need: calls, imports and references edges, plus string-literal edges (message texts matched by client regular expressions, storage keys, setting names, outbox kinds, route paths); impact is reverse reachability

competency_questions.question_form: CQ9 Where is item ID X (finding, ruling, card, limitation) defined and where is it cited?
competency_questions.example: grep the bottleneck compile for nine bottleneck IDs and print each card block; grep design notes and the plan for register IDs
competency_questions.how_often: Program 454 calls in 336 episodes and 308 transcripts; product 18 calls (plus ID greps counted under CQ2)
competency_questions.what_the_agent_did: Regular-expression greps over IDs, then awk or sed to print each defining block
competency_questions.what_a_graph_would_need: An entity node for every ID pattern, with defined_in and cited_in edges to document sections

competency_questions.question_form: CQ10 What changed here recently and why (commits, PRs, rulings)?
competency_questions.example: git log for a feature folder between two commits; list PR commits and checks
competency_questions.how_often: Product 151 calls in 110 episodes; program 460 calls
competency_questions.tokens_it_cost: Product 195k fetched, 4.3M carried (1.8%, the form v1's co-change test targets); program 13.3M carried
competency_questions.what_the_agent_did: git log --oneline with a path, git show --stat, gh pr view
competency_questions.what_a_graph_would_need: Nodes for commit, PR and ruling; touches edges at symbol level; dates; co-change as derived edges

competency_questions.question_form: CQ11 Which files exist here; where is the file for X?
competency_questions.example: ls a feature folder; find a file by name; wc -l a set of files
competency_questions.what_the_agent_did: ls, find, Glob and wc -l, usually chained with reads
competency_questions.what_a_graph_would_need: A file-tree index; a graph adds nothing

competency_questions.question_form: CQ12 What sections does document X have?
competency_questions.example: grep -n '^#' on the plan or a design document before reading a range
competency_questions.what_a_graph_would_need: A document outline (section tree with line spans and hashes), which is part of the CQ2 layer

competency_questions.question_form: CQ13 Where is the other half of a contract: route and client call, payload schema and client type, outbox kind and handler, storage key and reader?
competency_questions.example: Which response model the jobs router declares and which web provider function consumes it; which API paths and fields the phone sends for media upload
competency_questions.how_often: Product 58 calls in 49 episodes and 23 transcripts; program 99 calls
competency_questions.what_the_agent_did: Paired greps in the router or schemas and in the client API modules
competency_questions.what_a_graph_would_need: Route nodes (method, path); client call sites resolved to routes (v1 already has these links); schema-to-client-type links; outbox kind-to-handler links

competency_questions.question_form: CQ14 Does this file:line citation in a document still say what the document claims?
competency_questions.example: Print lines 151, 154, 158 and others of the invariants file and the cited lines of five source files to check a document's citations
competency_questions.how_often: Program 67 calls in 53 episodes; product 8 calls (rare as an explicit lookup; mostly documents are trusted without a check)
competency_questions.what_the_agent_did: Shell loops printing single cited lines
competency_questions.what_a_graph_would_need: cites edges from a document section to a code span, carrying the span's hash at citing time; a staleness flag pushed at edit time

competency_questions.question_form: CQ15 What table, migration or setting is behind X?
competency_questions.example: grep the config for a setting name and its readers; print the jobs models file
competency_questions.what_the_agent_did: Read models.py and migrations; grep settings names
competency_questions.what_a_graph_would_need: Nodes for table, column, migration and setting; reads, writes, migrates and reads_setting edges

competency_questions.question_form: CQ16 What do the build, CI, ops and lab scripts do and invoke?
competency_questions.example: Print the compile-gate script; print sections of the lab README; list UI texts and navigation targets to script the device lab
competency_questions.how_often: Product 264 calls in 182 episodes; program 540 calls
competency_questions.what_the_agent_did: Read whole scripts and README sections
competency_questions.what_a_graph_would_need: Mostly reading; a small graph of CI job to script to test command would help locate the right script

what_is_not_a_graph_question: Reading for understanding once the right span is known (the needed part of CQ3 orientation): a graph narrows what is read but does not replace reading it

Operations output: gate and test logs, background job output, CI status, git status, PR bodies being drafted, lab device dumps. Product: 512 calls, 22.9M carried and the largest lookup-step context (98.8M), because these are many small polling steps
Following instructions: skill and agent instruction files (product 10.0M carried, program 28.5M)
Checking a number or a string in a known place (grep -c, wc -l, one line by number)
Past-session transcripts (program 57M carried): measurement work on raw logs
Web pages and literature (program 48.6M carried) and third-party library source (program 6.5M): both outside the repository
Definitions (CQ5) and file location (CQ11): a symbol or file index answers these, and a graph adds nothing
counts: Transcripts scanned: 1,452 (28,229 model calls), split into product work 109 (28 with code edits: 13 main sessions and 15 test-writer subagents; 81 reviewer and code-reading subagents) and program work 1,343
Product: 3,124 lookup calls, 1,069 episodes (median 1 call, p90 7), 5.35M fetched tokens, 242M carried (23% of 1,040M context tokens), 468M lookup-step context (45%, overlapping carried)
Program: 19,024 lookup calls, 3,763 episodes (median 3 calls, p90 11), 47.9M fetched tokens, 1,147M carried (29% of 4,018M), 1,893M lookup-step context (47%, overlapping carried)
Chars per context token, measured: median 2.42 (quartiles 2.24 to 2.58) over 4,938 call pairs
Product carried by group: code orientation and definitions 38%, documents 18%, relational forms 20% (799 of 3,124 calls, 26%), non-graph 24%
13 main product sessions: lookups before the first code edit = 837k of 1,793k fetched tokens (47%) and 86.1M of 157.3M carried (55%)

Repeated orientation reads in product transcripts: design notes 106 calls in 46 transcripts (15.3M carried); gate defect IDs 83 calls in 40 transcripts (7.8M); plan section 0 in 15 transcripts (6.1M); handoff in 22 (3.2M); invariants file in 22 (1.2M)

Waste: empty searches 0.4% product and 0.5% program; same-window re-reads 2.2% and 2.6%; tool errors about 0.8% product; program exact cross-session duplicate reads about 12M fetched tokens (a quarter of program fetched, undercounted)
Batching: 86% of product lookups are shell commands, and 61% of those chain 2 or more lookups; program 50% shell, 64% of those chained
Rule-label accuracy, manual check: product 31-32 of 40, program 22-24 of 30
could_not_measure: Which lines of a read the agent actually used: only 9% of model calls carry visible text, so the 'never named again' share (40-60%) is a weak proxy
Intent for episodes with no visible text (most subagent episodes): it was inferred from the commands
Code version at session time (transcripts carry no commit SHA)
Whether a graph tool would change the calls: this is an observational count, and only an agent run can say
Exact cross-session duplicates when the same section is read under a different variable name (undercounted)
Several question forms inside one chained shell command: each call gets one form
The product sample is small (13 main sessions, one day, one plan); the mix of forms may differ for bug-fix or unplanned feature work

Primary texts I could not open: Grüninger and Fox 1995 (paper and chapter behind a login; only the authors' laboratory methodology page was read); Sillito, Murphy and De Volder 2008 TSE (only bibliographic records: 44 questions, 4 categories, two category names); Ko et al. 2007 (the PDF text is compressed and no PDF tool is on this machine). None of these were used for effect claims

v1_audit.summary: The v1 audit is written. v1 is a typed property graph built by static analysis. Its extraction is strong. Calls are never linked by name alone: 0 of 4,886 call edges were. They are resolved by Python scope and import binding, or by the TypeScript type checker. 1,373 of them (28.1 %) point to a name that two or more definitions share, so a resolver that matched by name alone would have had to guess on those. Sampled precision is 100 % for most edge kinds. Call recall was measured only on a 15-symbol probe, and 690 TypeScript calls made through parameters or destructured bindings get no edge. Retrieval is mostly improvised or simplified. Exact implementations of published methods: personalised PageRank, BM25 and reciprocal rank fusion. Chosen by hand: the degree-normalised ranking, the hub cuts, the per-class budgets, the edge weights (extractor confidence used as relevance), the 0.5 confidence floor, the 30-day half-life, the packer and every parameter value. The tuning had a design defect: every ranking was compared at 2 hops, where the median task's whole reach fits inside the 8,000-token answer (5,010 tokens used). There, no mode moved T1 primary by more than +0.014 over breadth-first order (se 0.033), and recall at 16,000 tokens was identical for all nine modes. The top of the list moved a lot: T1 MRR rose by 0.10 to 0.18, and T2 recall at 2,000 tokens rose by up to 0.178. At unbounded depth, where order decides the answer, breadth-first order was never run, and the rankings spanned only 0.023. At that chosen depth the traversal selects nothing: a query reaches a median of 66 % of nodes, and 97.9 % of nodes sit in one component once folder-membership edges are removed. Degree is moderately heavy-tailed: Gini 0.53, maximum 140, and production in-degree Gini 0.78. The hubs are dependency-injection providers, configuration, main.py and the busiest tables. Other measured gaps: minConf 0.5 drops 34 % of co-change pairs from traversal but not from PageRank. The recency weight is computed but no ranking reads it. Identity is the path plus qualified name, with renames not followed; following renames would add 1.7 % of co-change pair occurrences at the frozen commit. The cache replay is the one part built directly from documented theory (verifying traces and early cutoff). The notes include six concrete v2 recommendations, each with a test that can reject it. The first is supervised random walks; literature gains are +0.01 to +0.07 AUC, with precision@20 tied against logistic regression. None of the six needs an install.

parts.part: Node kinds and what has no node
parts.how_it_works_now: 25 node kinds, 5,464 nodes, with ids of the form path#Qualified.name. Constants are recognised only by an upper-case regex. Object members become nodes only when a variable holds them. Pydantic fields exist only in an experimental layer that is not loaded by default. Commits and PRs have no nodes.
parts.origin: Improvised schema grown lane by lane, not derived from competency questions. LocAgent's schema is a subset of it.
parts.measured_quality: Reference definitions with no node: 354 of 3,150 on held-out T1 (11.2 %), of which 252 (8.0 %) are variables or object members, and 364 of 4,162 on tuning T1. Held-out question 40 is answered empty because its member has no node.
parts.known_gap: No nodes for lower-case module variables, object members, schema fields, columns read, or commits and PRs.

parts.how_it_works_now: 36 default edge kinds plus 3 experimental. Python calls are resolved by stdlib ast binding: nested scopes, then module scope, then imports. Receiver types are inferred by hand for typed, self, singleton and chained_ctor calls. TypeScript uses the compiler's symbol resolution with no node_modules. URL literals are matched to routes. SQL table names are scanned from string literals. Documents are linked to code through a name dictionary, with a 1/k fan-out on ties.
parts.origin: Python is a simplified scope and type analysis in the PyCG family: no assignment-graph fixpoint, locals and parameters not checked, and a depth-first base walk instead of C3 method resolution order. TypeScript resolution is the compiler's own (published tool). URL, SQL and document linking are improvised.
parts.measured_quality: 0 of 4,886 call edges were chosen by name alone. 1,373 (28.1 %) point to a name that two or more definitions share, so binding matters. Sampled calls precision is 30 of 30, and 4,872 rows were machine-checked in the previous version. Precision for mentions is 27 of 30 and for constrains 19 of 20. 122 of 1,195 mention sites fan out to 2 to 5 candidates. Call recall: 37 of 37 on 15 symbols only. TypeScript has 690 calls through parameters or destructured bindings with no edge. Python has 2,148 unresolved call sites. 663 Python calls with inferred receiver types (404 of them onto a shared name) have precision not measured separately.
parts.known_gap: Call recall is unmeasured at scale, and no JS/TS call-graph benchmark exists. TypeScript takes declarations[0], which can be wrong with overloads or merged declarations. Extractor confidence is used as a ranking weight.

parts.how_it_works_now: A node's identity is its id string (path plus qualified name, or the test titles, with a ~2 suffix for duplicates). Each commit's graph is built from scratch. Co-change uses git log --no-renames over the paths that exist at the build commit.
parts.origin: Improvised name-based identity. Published alternatives were not used: git rename detection, origin analysis, CodeShovel and CodeTracker.
parts.measured_quality: Not measured inside v1. Measured here: 45 renames (41 of them code files) in 233 non-merge commits. Following them would add 138 file-pair occurrences to the 7,948 counted (+1.7 %) at the frozen commit. 58 code paths in history are absent at the frozen commit. Literature (Hora et al., ICSE 2018): 10-21 % of method-level changes are untracked in 15 Java systems.
parts.known_gap: A moved file or a renamed symbol becomes a new entity, and cached conclusions and history attached to the old id are orphaned.

parts.how_it_works_now: Built from non-merge ancestors, with same-PR siblings of the task dropped. Only commits touching 2 to 30 files count, and a pair needs support of 2 or more. Confidence = support / commits touching the source file. The recency weight is sum 0.5^(age/30 days). Edges are at file level, one row per direction. At the frozen commit: 177 commits used, 948 pairs.
parts.origin: Simplified ROSE (Zimmermann et al. 2004/2005): support, confidence and the 30-file cap come from ROSE. It is pair-only, with no multi-antecedent rules (TARMAQ) and no tangled-change filter. The 30-day half-life and min support 2 are improvised.
parts.measured_quality: All 948 pairs were reproduced independently. Adding the history class gave +0.056 base primary on tuning. On held-out, 50 % of typed recall came through a path containing a co-change edge. Outside mobile, the typed store could not be told apart from the co-change floor (+0.001 [-0.051, +0.056]).
parts.known_gap: No ranking reads the recency weight. minConf 0.5 removes 318 of the 948 pairs (34 %) from traversal, while PageRank uses all of them. Only the higher direction's confidence is kept. Renames are not followed.

parts.how_it_works_now: Modes: breadth-first k-hop; per-class budgets (a mixed-radix counter); and ordered metapaths (an automaton of typed steps with min and max repeats). Hub rules: in-degree greater than 5, 10 or 15 on non-structural edges from non-test sources; and a transport rule (functions called from 3 or more slices, plus structural nodes). A blocked node is reached but not expanded.
parts.origin: k-hop is published (RepoGraph, LocAgent). Metapaths are simplified from heterogeneous-network meta paths (PathSim; paper not opened), with reachability only and no normalised similarity. Budgets and hub rules are improvised. The hub rules resemble omnipresent-module removal and Aider's x0.1 multiplier, which has no published ablation.
parts.measured_quality: Tuning T1 primary by hop limit: 0.438 at 1, 0.664 at 2, 0.727 at 3, 0.768 at 4, 0.784 unbounded. One direction only scored about 0.45. Budgets scored 0.779 and 0.755. The single metapath scored 0.615. Hub cuts at 2 hops scored 0.599 (>5), 0.635 (>10) and 0.665 (transport), against a base of 0.664. Connectivity: without membership edges, 97.9 % of nodes are in one component. The code classes alone hold 85.4 % of files and 99.7 % of definitions in one component. The calls class alone holds 40.4 % of definitions. Degree Gini is 0.53 and production in-degree Gini 0.78. A tail exponent of about 3.1 to 3.5 is a weak fit, not proof of a power law.
parts.known_gap: At the chosen unbounded depth a query reaches a median of 3,633 of 5,464 nodes (66 %), so traversal selects nothing. Hub cuts only removed recall. The metapath shapes are hand-written.

parts.how_it_works_now: bfs orders by hop, then reach-DAG parent count, then id. degnorm is one pass down the shortest-path DAG, dividing by out-degree. ppr runs 40 power iterations with restart and dangling mass going to the seeds; arc weight is the extractor confidence, with co-change scaled by cochange_w. Also: a co-change sum, BM25 matching FTS5, and RRF with k=60. Engine-only modes: x_wsp, Louvain x_comm, x_prank and x_core.
parts.origin: Published and exact: PPR, BM25, and RRF (Cormack et al. 2009; k=60 fixed in a pilot, 'not critical'). Simplified: the co-change score (ROSE) and degnorm (spreading activation with no decay or threshold, propagating along shortest-path arcs only). Hand-picked: restart 0.30, weights 1 and 3, minConf 0.5, and the x_wsp costs. Louvain is used as an unseeded prior in an improvised way.
parts.measured_quality: Each mode minus bfs at 2 hops. T1 primary: +0.000 to +0.014 (se 0.033). T1 MRR: +0.10 to +0.18. T1 nDCG@10: +0.04 to +0.10. T2 recall at 2,000 tokens: +0.067 to +0.178. T2 MRR: +0.08 to +0.28. T1x primary: within ±0.004. Recall at 16,000 tokens is identical across all modes. At unbounded depth the modes span 0.7626 to 0.7853 (0.023, within one se), and bfs was not run there. The tuned degnorm pick scored 0.011 below the rule's first pick (4 hops, PPR) on held-out T1.
parts.known_gap: Every non-history edge has weight 1, and extraction certainty is used as relevance. Nothing is learned from the 388 tuning tasks. No ranking reads recency or the question kind.

parts.how_it_works_now: Stage 1: 40 configurations varied one factor at a time around a base of hops 2, both directions, base classes, PPR r0.30 and weight 1. Stage 2: 20 more hand-written after reading stage 1, each with a reason. Selection: highest T1 primary; then the lowest complexity within one se of the best; then tokens; then the configuration name.
parts.origin: One-factor-at-a-time screening is a published but weak design. The one-standard-error rule is published. The factor levels and the base are improvised; the base came partly from the first round's measurements on 45 commits.
parts.measured_quality: The design hid the interaction that matters: ranking can only matter when the reach exceeds the budget. The tie-break by name chose the weakest of 15 tied configurations (audit D3). Literature (Bergstra and Bengio 2012): random search is as good or better than grid search at a fraction of the cost.
parts.known_gap: Never tried: ranking at depths other than 2 and unbounded; bfs at unbounded depth; learned edge or question-kind weights; random or factorial search; commit cross-validation within tuning; per-runtime configurations; partial file outlines; diversity in the packed list.

parts.how_it_works_now: Ranked nodes are projected to files or symbols and padded with an optional tail. Items are laid down in rank order until the budget (2k, 4k, 8k or 16k tokens) is full. The last item is cut on whole lines and a footer is added. The file signature form lists every definition in the file. Tokens are counted with a regex approximation of a code tokenizer.
parts.origin: Improvised greedy prefix fill. Aider packs by binary search to land within 15 % of the budget. Knapsack or submodular budgeted selection, the published framing, was not used (not read in this pass).
parts.measured_quality: At the 2-hop base, T1 primary was 0.363 for snippets, 0.664 for signatures and 0.518 for symbol granularity.
parts.known_gap: No value-per-token choice and no redundancy control. One large outline can push out several smaller relevant files.

parts.how_it_works_now: A seed maps to its file plus its definition: by id, then name and line, then line, then up to 50 definitions inside the range. The DIR tail adds same-directory, capability-folder and parent-directory files. The CO tail adds files ordered by co-change count and recency, then DIR.
parts.origin: Improvised baselines that model what an agent would do.
parts.measured_quality: The CO tail added +0.107 at 2 hops. On held-out, scripted search drew 48 % of its recall from the CO tail. 105 of 418 held-out T1 tasks matched by file only, and 6 matched nothing.
parts.known_gap: Seed matching is the same in every arm, so it biases none, but some seeds fall back to the whole file.

parts.how_it_works_now: Eight hand-written SQL programs, one per question kind (screen to tables, tests that reach a function, invariants on a file, the other half, setting readers, migrations on a table, route clients, change reach). They use recursive CTEs with a depth cap of 12 and a shared target parser, and are ported to the graph engines.
parts.origin: Improvised metapath-style queries written after the schema existed, the reverse of competency-question design (Grüninger and Fox).
parts.measured_quality: Held-out, 30 questions: typed macro F1 0.745 against 0.645 for scripted search, +0.100 [-0.060, +0.257], inconclusive. The typed arms lost 'other half of a rule' by -0.306 F1 over 4 questions. Answers were about 31 tokens, against 695 tokens read by search. The cost of writing the programs is not counted.
parts.known_gap: Fixed programs cannot answer open questions, and schema holes show up as empty answers. No agent has used them.

parts.how_it_works_now: Each answer is stored with every node and edge it read (whole-record and semantic hashes), every query pattern with a hash of its matched set (negative dependencies), its files, and sub-results for early cutoff. Policies were replayed over 190 snapshots.
parts.origin: Published: verifying traces and early cutoff from build systems (Build systems à la carte, Salsa backdating, Skyframe change pruning, rustc red-green). The pattern-level negative dependency is sound but cites no source; the closest concept is predicate locks, not read in this pass.
parts.measured_quality: Fact level with patterns served 87.6 % of 29,097 lookups with 0 stale; read-field hashes served 95.9 % with 0 stale. File level served 86.5 % with 6.5 % stale (13.2 % on the questions whose answer changes). Without patterns, 6.8 % were stale. The whole-graph ranking could be served from cache for only 9-25 % of lookups. Zero stale is expected by construction and is judged against the extractor's own facts.
parts.known_gap: Only cheap deterministic answers were cached. Identity is the id string, so a rename invalidates an entry rather than carrying it over. Facts have no validity interval.

from_literature: Personalised PageRank with restart (Page, Brin et al.; Haveliwala), implemented exactly to SPEC 8.2
BM25 text ranking (Robertson et al.), copied exactly from SQLite FTS5
Reciprocal rank fusion with k=60 (Cormack, Clarke, Büttcher, SIGIR 2009; read: k fixed in a pilot, near-optimal, not critical)
Co-change support and confidence and the 30-file transaction cap from ROSE (Zimmermann et al. 2004/2005), in simplified pair-only form
k-hop ego-graph retrieval and the hop sweep, following RepoGraph and LocAgent
TypeScript call, import and render resolution by the TypeScript compiler's own symbol resolution
Python call resolution by scope, import and type analysis in the PyCG family (simplified: no fixpoint, no local shadowing check, depth-first base walk instead of C3)
Ordered metapaths, simplified from heterogeneous-network meta paths (PathSim): reachability only, no normalisation
Louvain communities (Blondel et al. 2008) as an optional prior in one engine arm
The cache replay's verifying traces and early cutoff (Build systems à la carte; Salsa; Skyframe; rustc)
Selection within one standard error of the best, preferring the simplest (the one-se rule)
Evaluation discipline: leak-free per-parent builds, a date split, held-out run once, bootstrap clustered by commit, and cheap floors as baselines
improvised: The schema: 25 node kinds and 36 edge kinds grown lane by lane, not derived from questions. Constants are found only by an upper-case regex; variables, object members and schema fields have no nodes in the default graph.
Edge weights: the extractor's confidence is used as relevance, and every non-history edge is weighted about 1
The confidence floor minConf 0.5, which removes 34 % of co-change pairs from traversal but not from PageRank
The 30-day half-life and minimum support of 2 for co-change; the recency weight is computed and never used by any ranking
Identity by path plus qualified name, with no rename tracking (--no-renames) and no identity across commits
Document-to-code linking through a name dictionary with six hand-made tie-break rules and 1/k fan-out
URL-to-route matching rules and SQL-literal table extraction
The degree-normalised ranking (one-pass spreading activation along the shortest-path DAG)
The hub rules: in-degree thresholds of 5, 10 and 15, and the transport rule (called from 3 slices)
Per-class traversal budgets and the hand-written metapath shapes
The kind costs for weighted shortest path in the engine arms
Every numeric parameter: restart 0.30, co-change weights 1 and 3, 40 iterations, and 2 hops as the base
The 60 configurations: one factor at a time around a hand-picked base, plus 20 picked after reading the first table, with ties broken by configuration name
The packer (rank-order prefix fill with a whole-file outline per item) and the regex tokenizer
The DIR and CO padding tails and the seed-mapping rules
The eight per-kind question programs and their depth cap of 12
The negative-dependency (query-pattern) record in the cache replay: sound in effect, but cited to no source
measured_gaps: Name resolution: 0 of 4,886 call edges were chosen by name alone. 1,373 (28.1 %) target a name with 2+ definitions, so a name-only resolver would have had to guess there. 663 Python calls rest on hand-made type inference (404 of them onto a shared name), with precision not measured separately. 122 of 1,195 document mention sites fan out to 2-5 candidates.

Call recall: measured only on 37 calls over 15 symbols. TypeScript has 690 calls through parameters or destructured bindings with no edge. Python has 2,148 unresolved call sites, 103 of which match the name of a repository definition.

Connectivity: without membership edges, 97.9 % of nodes, 89.3 % of files and 99.7 % of definitions are in one weakly connected component. The code classes alone hold 85.4 % of files and 99.7 % of definitions in one component. The calls class alone holds only 40.4 % of definitions in its largest component.

Degree: mean 5.8, median 3, p99 44, max 140, Gini 0.526, top 1 % of nodes hold 11.4 % of edge ends. Production in-degree: Gini 0.783, max 70, top 1 % hold 21.9 %. The approximate tail exponent of 3.1-3.5 over 58-82 nodes does not establish a power law. Hubs are the DI providers (get_session, get_current_principal, require_manager), core/config.py, main.py, the job and job_event tables, and AppContext.jsx.
Unbounded both-direction traversal reaches a median of 3,633 of 5,464 nodes (66 %) and 323 files per query, so traversal performs no selection at the chosen configuration.

Ranking vs bfs at 2 hops (tuning). T1 primary: +0.000 to +0.014 (se 0.033). T1 MRR: +0.10 to +0.18. T2 recall@2k: +0.067 to +0.178. T2 MRR: +0.08 to +0.28. Recall at 16k is identical for all modes, because the median reach (5,010 tokens) fits in 8k. At unbounded depth the rankings span 0.023 (within one se) and no bfs was run.
The tuned ranking (unbounded, degnorm) scored 0.011 below the rule's first pick (4 hops, PPR) on held-out T1 ([-0.004, +0.026]).
minConf 0.5 drops 318 of 948 co-change pairs (34 %) from traversal, while PageRank keeps them.
Renames: 45 in 233 non-merge commits. Following them would add 138 of 7,948 pair occurrences (+1.7 %) at the frozen commit, and 58 historical code paths are absent at the frozen commit.
11.2 % of held-out T1 reference definitions have no node (8.0 % variables and object members).

construction.summary: Lane finding: for this stack, v1's call-graph layer is close to its ceiling. I measured the residue on the repository without installing anything. TypeScript direct calls: 7 of 1,789 web call sites are recoverable by name, and giving the checker the React and React Native types changes resolved repo edges by 0 of 764. Python: 290 of 4,268 candidate call sites (6.8%) are unresolved with a repo-matching name, mostly generic names. Calls through parameters look large (445 mobile, 265 web), but 92% and 82% are React state setters. The real weak spot is the field-level cross-runtime link. v1's experimental response-field reads are name-keyed and only 12.6% of 1,183 have a single candidate field; the web app is untyped JavaScript (120 files, 1 with a type annotation). The literature supports a layered method. Use a type-aware resolver for references (the TypeScript checker, and mypy or Pyright for Python). Use dynamic test-run edges as ground truth and as an edge source (DyPyBench: static PyCG holds only 49% of dynamic edges). Use the framework's own export for routes, schemas and tables (FastAPI app.openapi()). Use coarse file-level dependencies plus dynamic data for 'what breaks' (Legunsen: method-level static selection was 10.6% unsafe and 55.7% imprecise, against 0.2% and 33.0% for class level). No study shows a better call graph improving agent success or tokens, and nothing measures SCIP or language-server data inside an agent. Code property graphs, Kythe, Glean and Jelly are not recommended at this size, and CodeQL is excluded by licence for a private repo. The notes file has the full evidence, the build design for field edges, the install list and the tests.

findings.claim: A static Python call graph (PyCG) holds only about half of the edges seen at run time, but most of the missing callees are built-in-type methods that do not matter for a repo graph.
findings.evidence: DyPyBench, 50 projects: PyCG ran on 39 (6 timed out at 6 hours, 3 exceeded 60 GB, 2 crashed); 49% of dynamic edges and 48.5% of dynamic callees are in PyCG's graph; 59% of missing callees are methods of built-in types; about 12% of mismatches are name-resolution differences; 95% of dynamic callers are in the static graph. Dynamic edges only cover what the tests run.
findings.source: Bouzenia et al., DyPyBench, FSE 2024 (arXiv 2403.00539), PDF text read
findings.strength: medium to strong (independent, 50 projects), about PyCG not about v1
findings.applies_at_this_size: The 6-hour and 60 GB failures were on much larger programs than this backend (v1's Python stage runs in 1.8 s). The 49% figure does not transfer to v1, which resolves through scopes, constructors and annotated receivers.

findings.claim: Reported Python call-graph precision and recall vary a lot by benchmark and mode, so the often-quoted 99.2% precision and 69.9% recall is not a safe expectation.
findings.evidence: PyCG authors: about 99.2% precision, about 69.9% recall (abstract only). Independent re-run on the PyCG micro-benchmark of 126 cases: 107 complete (84.9%), 110 sound (87.3%). Jarvis paper, 6 real applications: PyCG precision/recall 0.19/0.48 in one mode and 0.99/0.76 in another; Jarvis 0.35/0.60 and 0.99/0.82. Jarvis still misses functions stored in lists or dicts and reflective calls.
findings.source: PyCG arXiv 2103.00587 (abstract); Venkatesh et al. arXiv 2410.00603 (HTML read); Jarvis arXiv 2305.05949 v5 (HTML read)
findings.strength: medium (micro-benchmarks and authors' own comparisons)
findings.applies_at_this_size: Yes at this size, but these are research tools. v1 already resolves most of the same cases, so the numbers describe PyCG and Jarvis only.

findings.claim: For JavaScript, approximate interpretation (Jelly) raises call-edge recall from 75.9% to 88.1% at about 1.5% precision cost on Node.js libraries.
findings.evidence: 36 benchmarks with dynamic call graphs from test suites; 141 programs in total; 55.1% more call edges, 21.8% more reachable functions, 17.7% more resolved call sites; static analysis time rose under 10% for 76 of 141 programs and over 2x for 20; 9 ran out of memory. Per-call precision dropped up to 12.3 points on one project. Ground truth is test-suite coverage. SWARM-JS micro-benchmark: Jelly completeness 38.8%, soundness 67.4%.
findings.source: Laursen, Xu, Møller, PLDI 2024 (PDF text read); arXiv 2410.00603 for SWARM-JS
findings.strength: medium (single group, Node libraries; React, JSX and React Native not verified)
findings.applies_at_this_size: The gain is bounded here. In this repo the callback gap that points-to or hint-based analysis could fill is about 36 call sites in mobile and 47 in web.

findings.claim: Method-level static call-graph selection is worse than class-level for 'what breaks if this changes'; coarse dependencies plus dynamic data are as good as anything measured.
findings.evidence: 985 revisions of 22 Java projects, measured against Ekstazi: class-level static unsafe in 0.2% of revisions and imprecise in 33.0%; method-level unsafe in 10.6% and imprecise in 55.7%, and slower than running all tests. RTA selected the same tests as CHA. Ekstazi alone: 32% average time reduction (abstract).
findings.source: Legunsen et al., FSE 2016 (PDF text read); Gligoric et al., ISSTA 2015 (abstract)
findings.strength: medium (independent and large, but Java and JUnit, and safety is relative to Ekstazi)
findings.applies_at_this_size: Yes. Hundreds of files and commits is the same order as these projects; hub files select everything at file level, which is a precision limit.

findings.claim: Structure plus co-change history beats either alone for impact analysis, which supports v1's design.
findings.evidence: Combining conceptual and evolutionary coupling raised precision and recall by up to 17% and 41% over single sources on 4 open-source systems; structural coupling alone missed many ripple effects. Search snippets only.
findings.source: WCRE 2010 and ICSE 2012 impact analysis papers (search results, not opened)
findings.strength: weak to medium (snippets)
findings.applies_at_this_size: Yes.

findings.claim: SCIP is a transmission format with symbol resolution but no call edge or data flow, so a call graph from it must be derived by joining occurrences with the syntax tree.
findings.evidence: scip.proto: Occurrence with symbol_roles bit set (Definition, Import, WriteAccess, ReadAccess, Generated, Test, ForwardDefinition), enclosing_range, SymbolInformation relationships; DESIGN.md says it is not a storage or query format and non-goals include refactoring. Size and speed claims (4-5x smaller than LSIF; 8x smaller and 3x faster from one Meta engineer) are vendor observations with no controlled benchmark.
findings.source: github.com/sourcegraph/scip (proto and DESIGN.md read); Sourcegraph announcement post
findings.strength: strong for the schema description, weak for the performance claims
findings.applies_at_this_size: The size and speed benefits are irrelevant at 480 files. Only the indexers' resolution accuracy matters, and no measurement of it inside an agent exists.

findings.claim: v1's TypeScript call resolution is essentially complete for repo-internal direct calls, and the hermetic export without node_modules does not lose repo edges.
findings.evidence: Mobile program, 138 files, non-test calls 2,538: repo-definition edges 764 with and without library types; unresolved 689 to 11 but those became external library calls; test files 932 and 932; JSX repo components 31 and 31. Web app, 1,789 non-test calls: 241 unresolved, of which 6 match exactly one repo function name and 1 several. This refutes my hypothesis that missing types cost edges.
findings.source: My re-measurement with the TypeScript 5.3.3 checker already in technician-app/node_modules (scripts measure_ts.js and measure_web.js in the scratchpad folder g2c)
findings.strength: medium (direct measurement on this repo; counts resolution classes, not accuracy against a ground truth)
findings.applies_at_this_size: Specific to this repo at the current commit.

findings.claim: Calls through a parameter or destructured binding are mostly React state setters, so the real higher-order gap is small.
findings.evidence: Mobile 445 such calls: 409 set* names, 22 on* names, 380 from array destructuring of a hook; web 265: 218 set*, 19 on*, 218 from hook destructuring. Unexplained remainder: 14 mobile, 28 web.
findings.source: My measurement (param_names.js)
findings.strength: medium (direct measurement)
findings.applies_at_this_size: Specific to this repo.

findings.claim: v1's Python pass is not name matching only; its unresolved residue is 6.8% of in-repo candidate call sites, mostly generic names.
findings.evidence: Re-run of v1's py_extract.py on the current backend/, 13,572 call sites: 6,116 external, 3,978 resolved (2,337 by name in scope, 777 constructors, 608 typed receivers, 153 self, 76 module, 17 chained constructors, 10 singletons), 290 unresolved but the called name matches a repo definition, 2,989 unresolved and matching nothing. Top residue: result.scalars 25, session.commit 9, counts.get 8 (generic) and service.record_punch 7, service.record_presence 6 (genuine). Older cached build: 103 of about 2,600.
findings.source: My run of facts/py_extract.py on a git archive of backend/ at HEAD
findings.strength: medium (v1's own statistics; no independent resolver run)
findings.applies_at_this_size: Specific to this repo. Calls through aliases or getattr could hide in the 2,989 'other' sites and cannot be counted without an independent resolver.

findings.claim: The field-level cross-runtime link is v1's weakest extraction: 87% of response-field reads are ambiguous, the web side has no types, and only a small part can be resolved exactly today.
findings.evidence: v1 experimental response_fields: 1,183 read edges (625 mobile, 558 web) to 390 fields; candidates per read: 1 -> 149 (12.6%), 2 -> 148, 3 -> 120, 4 -> 216, 5 -> 65, 6 or more -> 485 (41%). Mobile checker-exact reads: 194 reads to 58 distinct fields of interfaces named like backend models, out of 3,589 non-test property accesses (lower bound; destructured reads not counted). Only 21 of 110 backend schema classes have a same-named exported TypeScript type. Web: 120 JS files, 1 with JSDoc, 0 TypeScript.
findings.source: v1 cache experimental/response_fields.edges.jsonl; my measure_fields.js and git ls-files
findings.strength: medium (direct measurement)
findings.applies_at_this_size: Specific to this repo.

findings.claim: The framework can export its own exact route, schema and injection description, which makes static inference of those facts unnecessary.
findings.evidence: FastAPI documents a public app.openapi() method that builds the schema from app.routes and puts Pydantic response models in components/schemas, callable without a server. APIRoute carries dependant, response_model, endpoint, dependencies and operation_id at master (semi-private, pin the version). The repo has 63 response_model uses. Static REST-spec inference from Java server code (Respector, AutoOAS) and microservice endpoint recovery (three of the tools detected no endpoint, best F1 0.79) are the documented hard case, from snippets only.
findings.source: FastAPI docs 'Extending OpenAPI' and fastapi/routing.py (read); Respector/AutoOAS and arXiv 2412.08352 (search snippets)
findings.strength: strong for the mechanism (official docs and source); weak for the static-inference comparison (snippets)
findings.applies_at_this_size: Yes at any size.

findings.claim: Code property graphs and program slicing have no measured benefit for agent context retrieval; the only agent-side evidence is a weak-model single run.
findings.evidence: CPG spec 1.1 has AST, CFG, call graph, dominators and PDG (REACHING_DEF, CDG) layers; the 2014 paper's result is 18 new Linux-kernel vulnerabilities. Joern: JDK 21, frontends pysrc2cpg and jssrc2cpg (TypeScript not named); type recovery for dynamic languages described as work in progress in 2024 issues (snippet). ARISE: statement-level intra-procedural def-use edges added to SWE-agent with Qwen2.5-Coder-32B on SWE-bench Lite (300 tasks): resolve rate 22.0% (+4.7 points), function recall at 1 from 0.43 to 0.60; abstract only, no token figures. Katana (snippet) cut average bug-fix context from 39 to 15 lines.
findings.source: cpg.joern.io spec; docs.joern.io; github.com/joernio/joern; Yamaguchi et al. IEEE S&P 2014; arXiv 2605.03117 abstract; arXiv 2205.00180 snippet
findings.strength: weak
findings.applies_at_this_size: Whole-program slicing is too coarse for 'what breaks'; only intra-procedural def-use for field reads has any support.

findings.claim: No controlled ablation of file versus definition versus statement granularity inside an agent exists, so granularity has to be tested here.
findings.evidence: A targeted search found only designs: Aider file-level map, LocAgent function-level, RepoGraph line-level, ARISE statement-level, CoSIL two-stage file then function; no ablation. The earlier round's read-displacement finding (maps that return code bodies let agents skip Read calls) suggests the returned unit matters more than the edge unit.
findings.source: Web search results; prior round widen/lane-agents.md
findings.strength: weak (absence of evidence from searches)
findings.applies_at_this_size: Yes.

findings.claim: Dynamic call recording is cheap to add in Python 3.12 and gives the strongest published ground truth for call edges and test-to-code edges.
findings.evidence: sys.monitoring (Python 3.12) offers PY_START, PY_RETURN and CALL events with per-location DISABLE, which the docs call very important for performance (no figure given). coverage.py dynamic_context=test_function records which lines each test ran into SQLite. DynaPyt recording averaged 215 minutes per project in DyPyBench (includes instrumentation of larger suites).
findings.source: docs.python.org sys.monitoring; coverage.readthedocs.io contexts; DyPyBench
findings.strength: medium (mechanism documented; overhead not measured)
findings.applies_at_this_size: The project's tests need Postgres for integration tests; the repo already has a Docker gate with Postgres.

findings.claim: CodeQL is excluded for this repository by its licence.
findings.evidence: CodeQL CLI LICENSE.md: free for academic research and for analysing open-source codebases (automation allowed for open-source on GitHub); use with a non-open-source codebase, or in CI or automated analysis elsewhere, needs a paid GitHub Advanced Security licence.
findings.source: github.com/github/codeql-cli-binaries LICENSE.md (read)
findings.strength: strong
findings.applies_at_this_size: Yes.

recommendations.what: Measure v1's extraction recall and precision before changing anything: run an independent resolver (scip-typescript, scip-python or Pyright) and a recorded dynamic call graph, then score v1's calls, imports, defines and test_calls_route edges against both. Read 60 disagreeing edges by hand.
recommendations.from_theory: Dynamic ground truth and independent-tool agreement, as in Jelly and DyPyBench.
recommendations.expected_effect: Shows whether extraction is a bottleneck at all. My measurements predict under 7% Python residue and about 0 for TypeScript direct calls, with disagreement concentrated in framework-invoked code and aliasing.
recommendations.how_to_test_on_tuning_data: Per tuning commit, compute v1 recall and precision against dynamic in-repo edges and against the resolver. If v1 recall on dynamic in-repo edges is at or above 95%, stop extraction work. Disagreements are hand-labelled for who was right.
recommendations.needs_install: scip-typescript (npm, Apache-2.0), scip-python (npm, Pyright fork, Node 16+ and Python 3.10+, licence text not confirmed), the scip CLI (Apache-2.0) or Pyright alone (MIT); coverage.py optional because Python 3.12 has sys.monitoring built in. Sizes not stated on the pages read. Run offline in a Linux container after one install fetch; scip-python needs an --environment JSON to avoid calling pip.
recommendations.replaces_in_current_graph: Nothing; closes the never-measured gap.

recommendations.what: Record dynamic edges from the Python test run (sys.monitoring or coverage per-test contexts) and store them as exercised_by (test to definition) and called_at_runtime edges, run in the project's Docker image with Postgres.
recommendations.from_theory: Ekstazi-style dynamic dependencies; dynamic call graphs as ground truth (DyPyBench, Jelly).
recommendations.expected_effect: An exact 'which tests touch this definition' answer and edges for framework-invoked handlers that no static call graph finds. Limit: it covers only what the tests execute.
recommendations.how_to_test_on_tuning_data: On tuning commits, check whether adding these edges raises recall of tests that failed or changed with the change at equal answer size over the file-level baseline; time the suite with and without recording.
recommendations.needs_install: None beyond the project's own container; coverage.py (Apache-2.0, small) optional.
recommendations.replaces_in_current_graph: The 39 test_calls_route edges and file-level test links as the only test evidence.

recommendations.what: Replace AST detection of routes, response models, tables and dependency injection by the framework's own export: import the FastAPI app with stub environment variables, write app.openapi() and walk app.routes (handler qualified name, file and line through inspect, dependencies, response model), and read SQLAlchemy mapper metadata. Keep the AST edges as a cross-check.
recommendations.from_theory: Runtime reflection is exact by construction where static inference is the documented hard case; the OpenAPI schema is a public interface.
recommendations.expected_effect: Removes any route or model the AST missed, adds dependency trees and required-field flags. The true route and model counts are unknown today (v1 found 77 routes and 110 schema classes).
recommendations.how_to_test_on_tuning_data: Diff against v1's route, table and depends_injects edges on every tuning commit; every difference is a defect in one side and is read by hand. Pin the FastAPI version because APIRoute.dependant is semi-private.
recommendations.needs_install: None; uses the backend's own dependencies from pyproject in the existing Docker image. Risk is import side effects.
recommendations.replaces_in_current_graph: py_extract.py's route, model, table and Depends detection (registers_route, returns_model, maps_table, depends_injects).

recommendations.what: Build three-tier field-level contract edges: (1) backend schema fields from the OpenAPI export; (2) mobile reads resolved by the TypeScript checker to client interface properties, with each client interface aligned to a schema once, by name or by structural overlap, plus drift edges for fields declared on one side only; (3) web reads found by a small intra-procedural def-use pass from the result of an API call already linked by URL, with candidates restricted to that operation's response schema. Unresolvable accesses (string-built keys, generic form components) are marked unresolved, not guessed.
recommendations.from_theory: Interface-description-based cross-language linking; checker-resolved property access; def-use for field flow (supported only narrowly: ARISE abstract, weak).
recommendations.expected_effect: Raises unique-candidate reads from 12.6% to the share the tiers cover. I will not state that share before building it. Today the exact tier already gives 194 mobile reads to 58 fields as a lower bound.
recommendations.how_to_test_on_tuning_data: Take tuning commits whose diff adds, removes or renames a field in a schemas.py; ground truth is the client files changed in the same pull request. Score precision and recall of predicted client files at equal answer size for v1 name-keyed, co-change only, and the three tiers. If the tiers do not beat co-change only, drop them.
recommendations.needs_install: None for tiers 1 to 3. Optional openapi-typescript (npm, MIT) to generate canonical types for a structural drift check; whether it runs on a local schema file offline was not confirmed on its page.
recommendations.replaces_in_current_graph: The experimental name-keyed reads_response_field edges (1,183 edges, 12.6% single-candidate).

recommendations.what: Resolve the 290 residual Python call sites with mypy's resolved trees: mypy.build.build with export_types, falling back to dmypy inspect --show definition (documented, experimental).
recommendations.from_theory: Type-aware resolution narrows candidates that name matching leaves ambiguous; mypy strict already runs in CI so annotations are broad. No published accuracy for mypy as a call resolver.
recommendations.expected_effect: Turns the genuine misses such as service.record_punch into edges; small, at most part of 6.8% of candidates.
recommendations.how_to_test_on_tuning_data: Hand-label 60 random residual sites; count how many mypy resolves correctly and how many wrongly. Pin the mypy version because the build API is internal.
recommendations.needs_install: None; mypy is already a project dev dependency.
recommendations.replaces_in_current_graph: The name-only residue in py_extract.py (calls_unresolved_name_matches_repo_def).

recommendations.what: Add a one-hop callback binding rule for TypeScript: a JSX attribute onX={handler} binds the child's onX() call to the handler.
recommendations.from_theory: Higher-order call resolution restricted to the deterministic one-hop case, because points-to or approximate interpretation is bounded here by about 41 on* call sites.
recommendations.expected_effect: About 41 call edges (22 mobile and 19 web on* calls); minor.
recommendations.how_to_test_on_tuning_data: Hand-check 30 added edges for precision; run only if the measurement step shows callbacks matter.
recommendations.replaces_in_current_graph: Nothing; passes_callable is Python-only today.

recommendations.what: Run a granularity test with three arms on identical tuning tasks: file-level edges and file cards; definition-level edges and cards (signature plus exact line range); definition-level plus field-level contract nodes. Measure agent tokens for the same correct result.
recommendations.from_theory: RTS evidence that coarse dependencies match dynamic selection and method level is worse (medium, Java); the earlier round's read-displacement finding; no agent ablation exists.
recommendations.expected_effect: Decides which edge and return granularity to build before more extraction work. Working hypothesis: file-level edges for impact and test selection, definition cards as the returned unit, field-level only where a contract exists.

earlier_research_missed: Round 1 (lane-algorithms) told the owner to expect Python call recall around 70% (PyCG's own abstract number); the verifier marked it not confirmed and it does not describe v1, which is not PyCG. Independent numbers disagree by method: 49% of dynamic edges in DyPyBench but 59% of the misses are built-in-type methods irrelevant to a repo graph, and recall 0.48 to 0.76 on six applications in the Jarvis paper.

Round 1 retrieved no JavaScript or TypeScript call-graph precision or recall; Jelly's figures (recall 75.9% to 88.1%, per-call precision cost about 1.5%) now exist, but from Node.js libraries, not React or React Native.

Neither round measured what v1's extractors lose. I bounded it from v1's own statistics and a checker re-measurement (no independent tool installed): Python residue 6.8% of candidates, TypeScript direct-call residue about 0.4% in the web app, and the hypothesis that the hermetic export loses edges for lack of node_modules is refuted (764 repo edges with and without library types).

Neither round noticed that the web app is untyped JavaScript (120 files, 1 with a type annotation), which decides how field-level links must be built, or that v1 already has an experimental field-link stage whose candidate sets are 87% ambiguous and sit outside the 37 edge kinds the retrieval used.
Neither round tested the framework's own export (FastAPI openapi and route table, SQLAlchemy metadata) as an extraction source, the cheapest exact source in the stack.

Neither round considered dynamic test-run edges as a source or as ground truth, although the call-graph literature uses them as the standard ground truth. The test-to-code evidence in v1 is 39 route-call edges.

The graphify lane describes cross-file resolution passes on a tree-sitter graph; tree-sitter does no name resolution and I did not verify how graphify resolves calls. v1's TypeScript pass is already type-resolved.
No granularity ablation exists in the agent literature (searched again here), and the earlier rounds treated granularity as settled.
could_not_verify: scip-python's licence beyond a LICENSE file that carries Pyright's MIT text; installed sizes of every tool listed; how scip-typescript resolves references (the README does not say).

Pyrefly call hierarchy support; Joern's TypeScript handling and type-recovery accuracy (frontends page lists JavaScript only; recovery status from issue snippets); Kythe's Python and TypeScript indexers and cross-language edges; whether Glean's Python indexer is open source (README lists it both ways).
CodeQL's framework models (the language-guide page does not say).

Primary text for Ekstazi tests-selected figures, HyRTS, Katana, the npm taint-slicing paper, Respector, AutoOAS, the microservice recovery comparison, the AngularJS cross-language study (93.2% recall) and Antal et al. SCAM 2018: search results or abstracts only.
What the application-wide and exhaustive mode labels mean in the Jarvis table, beyond the column headings.

Binkley, Gold and Harman's average slice size; whether Jelly handles JSX and React Native; the SQLAlchemy Mapper accessor names (the page did not state them); mypy's build.build stability across versions.
