modelling.summary: Method, derived from the documented theory and tested against this repository's own cached facts. (1) Schema from competency questions (Gruninger and Fox via Uschold and Gruninger 1996; Noy and McGuinness; Keet and Khan 2024): take the 16 measured questions CQ1-CQ16, type them (all validating), stratify them, write each as a metapath on a network schema (heterogeneous-information-network theory), keep only node and relation kinds some question uses (forward check), and require every question to have a path in the schema (backward check, the cheap analogue of the completeness theorems). Run against v1: all 36 edge kinds at the frozen commit serve some question, but v1's schema has no path for five of the 16 questions (CQ1 conclusions, CQ2 plan structure, CQ6 change sets, CQ10 recent history and why, CQ14 does a cited line still say that) and only a partial path for CQ4 (rules) and CQ9 (item ids). The code half is justified; the missing parts are history with reasons, items and decisions, rules with roles, claims with evidence, and spans with hashes. The method cannot say which of two valid designs is cheaper for an agent: the source itself says equivalent designs must be compared on other criteria, here agent tokens. (2) Hyperedges: right for a change set, a rule with role-carrying anchors, a claim with its dependency set and a test whose reach depends on a replaced dependency; not needed for calls, imports, reads, writes, citations, and a route is already the right n-ary node (identity is method plus path). Measured on v1: 85% of used commits touch more than 2 files; the 12% of commits with 16-30 files make 55% of pairwise co-change incidences; 49% of 1,896 co-change edges rest only on commits of 10+ files. No source measures hyperedge against pairwise for coding-agent retrieval. (3) Identity: separate entity key, occurrence and lineage; key by contract key, never-reused ids (ADR rule) or minted id plus alias table; never by line number or ordinal. Measured: v1's section, URL-site and invariant ids contain line numbers or ordinals; only 74-76% of section ids from 16-23 days earlier survive, 5 or 6 of 6 invariant ids now mean a different rule, 13 section ids and 11 invariant ids silently re-pointed over 110 transitions; definition ids are stable (99.0% at 16 days, 90.3% at 55 days) and a 0.8 body match recovers only 4 of 44 and 9 of 53 lost definitions at 55-57 days but 70 of 127 across the June restructuring. (4) Meaning layer: Document, Section, Item, Rule, Decision, Claim, Evidence, Source with relations defines, cites (span plus hash at citing), constrains (role), justified_by, supersedes, rests_on, about; computed statuses (valid, suspect, superseded, unanchored); ambiguity and not-in-repo as statuses rather than k edges of weight 1/k; refuted claims kept with a deprecated rank. Quality: Hogan's dimensions plus sampled accuracy (73-385 labels per heuristic edge kind), calibrated confidence split from strength, constraint violations counted. Whether any of this lowers agent tokens is untested; evidence on model-written or cached context about code is mixed to negative.

findings.claim: Competency questions are the documented requirements device and the method prescribes stratification, a forward pruning rule and a completeness check, but it gives no objective criterion for a good schema and no outcome evidence.
findings.evidence: Uschold and Gruninger 1996 (text extracted): questions should be stratified, 'not a well-designed ontology if all competency questions have the form of simple lookup queries'; for every object, attribute, relation and axiom there should first be a question that requires it; two designs that both answer a question are equivalent for it and 'any comparison must use other criteria'. Noy and McGuinness: questions are a sketch and a litmus test; 'no one correct way'. Keet and Khan 2024: very limited guidance on good CQs; scoping CQs need not be answerable, validating CQs must be; 438 CQs annotated. Wisniewski 2019 (summary): 234 CQs, 106 patterns, no 1:1 mapping from question to formal query.
findings.source: Uschold and Gruninger, AIAI-TR-191 (1996); Noy and McGuinness KSL-01-05 (2001); arXiv 2412.13688; J. Web Semantics 59 (2019) summary; Gruninger and Fox 1995 could not be opened
findings.strength: strong as discipline; weak as evidence of effect on a downstream task
findings.applies_at_this_size: Fully: 16 questions, a few dozen types, checks are scripts; scales with the number of questions, not nodes.

findings.claim: Against its own 16 measured competency questions v1's schema has no type path for five and a partial path for two; every one of its 36 edge kinds serves at least one question.
findings.evidence: Backward check of CQ1-CQ16 (use-cases.md section 5) against the frozen commit's node and edge kinds: no claim, evidence, phase, decision or commit node; commits exist only inside the attribute list of co_changed edges, with no message; cites edges carry no span hash; invariants have constrains edges with only token and how, no role, rationale or justified_by. Forward check: all 36 present kinds map to a CQ; weakest are same_capability (24), migration_follows (45), mocks (93), registers_screen/navigates (60), contains/defines (4,733) and pairwise co_changed (1,896).
findings.source: Own analysis of build/facts/cache/a31924a (nodes.jsonl, edges.jsonl) against use-cases.md
findings.strength: strong for the counts on this repository (full enumeration)
findings.applies_at_this_size: Yes; this is this repository's schema.

findings.claim: On v1's own facts the pairwise commit expansion is dominated by sweeping commits.
findings.evidence: 177 usable commits (2-30 files): median 7 files; 150 (85%) touch more than 2 files; commits of 16-30 files are 12% of commits and 55% of the 8,411 pair incidences; 8-15 files 30% of commits and 36%; 49% (930) of 1,896 co_changed edges are supported only by commits of 10+ files. v1 confidence is support over commits touching the source file and does not account for commit size.
findings.source: Own measurement, hyper.py over commits.jsonl and edges.jsonl of the frozen commit
findings.strength: strong for the counts; says nothing yet about whether size-aware weighting improves retrieval
findings.applies_at_this_size: Yes; at 100x history the clique form becomes millions of edges (435 pairs per 30-file commit).

findings.claim: The theory gives a principled weighting for a change set modelled as a hyperedge, and the closest software precedent caps transaction size.
findings.evidence: Zhou, Huang, Scholkopf NIPS 2006: a hyperedge as a clique with weight w(e)/delta(e); the natural random walk picks an incident hyperedge proportional to w(e) then a node uniformly; a plain graph 'cannot tell us whether the same person is the author of three or more articles'. ROSE (Zimmermann et al., ICSE 2004): transaction = set changed together, rules between entity sets, ignores changes affecting more than 30 entities; predicts 26% of further files and 15% of functions, top three suggestions correct 64% (ICSE text; TSE abstract reports over 70% on eight projects). Fatemi et al. IJCAI 2020: star-to-clique 'loses information'; 61% of original Freebase relations are non-binary. StarE: about 17.4% of 734M Wikidata statements have qualifiers; qualifier-aware models gain up to 25 MRR points on link prediction.
findings.source: papers read as extracted PDF text: NIPS 2006 Zhou et al.; ICSE 2004 ROSE; arXiv 1906.00137; arXiv 2009.10847
findings.strength: strong as mathematics (Zhou); medium for ROSE and link-prediction results (own evaluations, other domains); no study measures hyperedge against pairwise for coding-agent retrieval
findings.applies_at_this_size: Benefit here is weighting and meaning (message, PR), not space.

findings.claim: v1's identifiers for document sections, URL sites and invariants are positional and break within weeks, some silently re-pointing at a different entity; definition ids are much more stable.
findings.evidence: v1 ids: sec:<path>#L<line>, inv:CLAUDE.md#<ordinal>, urlsite:<path>:<line>:<method path>. Over 110 consecutive snapshot pairs: 335 of 29,643 section ids removed (1.13%), 260 of them reappearing under the same heading with a new id; 13 section ids kept but pointing at a different heading; 184 of 9,450 URL-site ids removed (1.95%), all reappearing; 11 of 553 invariant ids kept but a different rule. Against the frozen commit: section ids from 16 and 23 days earlier survive 76.0% and 74.4%; URL sites 54.0% and 48.0%; 5 of 6 (and at 27 days 6 of 6) old invariant ids now mean a different rule. Definitions: functions 99.0% (16 days), 97.6% (34), 90.3% (55); methods and classes 100%.
findings.source: Own measurement over 191 cached snapshots: idchurn.py, idcum.py (scratchpad lm/)
findings.strength: strong for the counts; sparse non-regular sample of history on one repository
findings.applies_at_this_size: Yes; this is the repository the graph is for.

findings.claim: Of definitions lost over 55-64 days, a name key proposes few successors and a body match of 0.8 recovers a minority except across a large restructuring; pure renames are rare.
findings.evidence: At 57 and 55 days: 44 and 53 lost; name exists elsewhere for 9 and 15; body match >=0.8 for 4 and 9 (different name in 1 and 4); 22 and 24 in a 0.5-0.8 band; 17 and 18 below 0.5; 20 and 20 sit in vanished files with the name gone. At 64 days (June restructuring): 70 of 127 match >=0.8 (2 under a different name). Per transition 76 of 102 removed function ids reappear under the same name and signature in another file. One threshold, difflib ratio, no blocking, no false-merge count.
findings.source: Own measurement: idlost.py, idbody.py, idbody2.py
findings.strength: strong for the counts; weak for generalising the matcher (one threshold, untuned)
findings.applies_at_this_size: Quadratic body comparison is trivial at about 1,800 definitions (minutes in plain Python); needs blocking at 10x.

findings.claim: No published method-history tool is established for this stack: they are evaluated on Java only and independent re-evaluations give lower numbers than the originals.
findings.evidence: HistoryFinder (arXiv 2507.14716) on a 200-method Java oracle, commit-level precision/recall/F1 percent: CodeShovel 93.44/84.17/88.56; CodeTracker 96.40/93.34/94.84; HistoryFinder 96.40/98.34/97.36; IntelliJ 58.82/77.43/66.85; git log -L by range 49.03/76.74/59.84, by function name 41.33/68.99/51.69; HistoryFinder matches by signature then body similarity (70% same file, 75% across files). PyRef (Python refactoring detector): precision 89.6% recall 76.1% by its authors, F1 0.64 in an independent 2025 comparison (summaries). Hora et al. ICSE 2018 (via v1 audit): 10-21% of method-level changes untracked in 15 Java systems.
findings.source: arXiv 2507.14716 (read); git-diff, git-log and git-patch-id documentation (read); PyRef and Hora summaries
findings.strength: medium (independent re-evaluation, Java only)
findings.applies_at_this_size: Tool is not needed; a deterministic ladder over git -M and body similarity suffices and can be measured here.

findings.claim: Published code schemas reuse well for structure, not for identity, and none models rules, decisions or claims for agents.
findings.evidence: Kythe VName includes path and its signature 'does not necessarily need to be stable across different versions'; SCIP symbol includes package version and path-derived descriptors, no field covers renames; Software Heritage ids are intrinsic content hashes for immutable objects; CPG layers are structural (CFG, PDG) with no question here needing them; CodexGraph's 6 node and 5 edge types were 'empirically designed', no schema ablation, and cost 22.16k tokens against 1.47k for BM25 on CrossCodeEval Lite and 102.25k against 14.76k on SWE-bench Lite (EM 27.90 vs 21.20 for BM25 on CrossCodeEval Lite; SWE-bench Lite resolved equal to AutoCodeRover at 22.96%).
findings.source: kythe.io/docs/schema; scip.proto; cpg.joern.io; arXiv 2408.03910 (read); Software Heritage docs via search summary
findings.strength: medium to strong as descriptions; weak for effect
findings.applies_at_this_size: Reuse the SCIP descriptor grammar as the textual form of a qualified name and the Kythe occurrence/entity split; do not adopt their identity.

findings.claim: Property graph is the right base model here; the useful borrowings from RDF are patterns (qualified relations, named graphs), not the stack.
findings.evidence: Hogan et al. 2021 section 3.3: reification does not assert the edge; named graph most flexible; RDF-star least flexible without edge ids (cannot pair a person's two terms with their start and end dates); property graph attaches context as edge attributes. W3C n-ary note: use a relation node for attributes on a relation, several participants with no primary, ordered arguments; creating classes for n-ary relations 'creates a maintenance problem'. PROV-O qualification pattern keeps the plain edge and adds a node for the details. GQL published as ISO/IEC 39075:2024; SQL/PGQ is SQL:2023 part 16; PG-Schema abstract says schema support in graph databases is 'limited'.
findings.source: arXiv 2003.02320 (read sections 3.2, 3.3, 7); W3C n-ary relations note (read); W3C PROV-O (read); PG-Schema arXiv 2211.10962 abstract; ISO catalogue summaries
findings.strength: strong as standards and survey; no outcome data
findings.applies_at_this_size: Yes: one publisher, no reasoning need, edges need their own evidence and status properties.

findings.claim: Metapaths are the right artifact for a schema derived from questions; PathSim and learned path weights exist but do not control answer size and no question here asks for similar peers.
findings.evidence: Shi et al. TKDE 2017: network schema is a directed graph over types, a meta path is a path on the schema defining a composite relation, similarity depends on the path (students versus same-field researchers). PathSim (VLDB 2011): s(x,y)=2*paths(x,y)/(paths(x,x)+paths(y,y)) defined for symmetric paths between same-type objects; denominator is visibility, damping hubs. Lao and Cohen 2010 (summary): one weight per edge-label sequence, beats random walk with restart on eight biology tasks. Meng et al. WWW 2015 (summary): discover meta paths from example pairs; selection intractable, greedy used.
findings.source: arXiv 1511.04854 (read); PVLDB vol 4 p992 (read); Machine Learning 81 (2010) and WWW 2015 summaries
findings.strength: strong as theory; evidence is bibliographic and biology networks, not code
findings.applies_at_this_size: Schema graph of about 25 types: yes. PathSim: no question needs it.

findings.claim: v1's confidence field mixes three different quantities and is not calibrated; the literature separates correctness probability from strength and calibrates by method class.
findings.evidence: Frozen-commit values: calls 1 (4,176), 0.9 (599), 0.95 (111); mentions 0.9, 1, 0.5, 0.6, 0.25, 0.33; constrains 1 (44) and 1/k values 0.09-0.12 for 38 edges chosen by ambiguous file; co_changed support ratios 1 to 0.12. Knowledge Vault: extractor scores 'are not necessarily on the same scale, and cannot necessarily be interpreted as probabilities'; Platt scaling on a validation set made predicted 0.9 correspond to about 90% true over 1.6B triples. Wikidata separates references (where) from ranks (which to trust).
findings.source: Own count of edges.jsonl; Dong et al. KDD 2014 (read); Wikidata Help:Ranking and Help:Sources (read)
findings.strength: strong for the v1 counts; medium for the calibration principle (one web-scale system)
findings.applies_at_this_size: Yes; at a few hundred labels bin by method class and give Wilson intervals instead of fitting Platt.

findings.claim: Knowledge-graph quality has a standard taxonomy and sampling theory that make accuracy cheap to estimate at this size; v1's 20-30 edge samples are too small.
findings.evidence: Hogan section 7: accuracy (syntactic, semantic, timeliness), coverage (schema, property, population, linkability completeness; representativeness), coherency (consistency, validity as violations per constraint), succinctness. Gao et al. PVLDB 2019: accuracy estimated by sampling triples clustered by entity with a margin of error; annotation cost c1 per entity plus c2 per triple; up to 60% cost reduction static, 80% evolving. My arithmetic: n = 1.96^2 p(1-p)/e^2 gives 385 labels for plus or minus 5 points with p unknown and 73 with p near 0.95; 20-30 labels give about plus or minus 10-20 points.
findings.source: arXiv 2003.02320 section 7 (read); PVLDB 12(11) 2019 (read); arithmetic is mine
findings.strength: strong as taxonomy and survey statistics; Gao medium to strong at web scale
findings.applies_at_this_size: Yes; about 73-385 labels per heuristic edge kind, parser-exact kinds need less.

findings.claim: The document-to-code binding is a known deterministic problem with high published precision, and v1's ambiguity handling (k edges of weight 1/k) discards the NIL and ambiguous cases the entity-linking model keeps as statuses.
findings.evidence: Dagenais and Robillard ICSE 2012: identifies code-like terms and links them using context because 'code elements mentioned in documents are rarely fully qualified'; average recall and precision 96% on four open source systems (Java). v1: 1,195 mention sites, 122 fan out to 2-5 candidates at 1/k, strict precision 27 of 30; 517 of 1,268 file tokens not in repo, 87 ambiguous, 85 ids defined in more than one document. DocRef (summary): over 1,000 documentation errors in five libraries, false alarms about 40% per a third-party summary. Entity linking surveys include NIL prediction.
findings.source: ICSE 2012 text (read); v1 audit and schema lane counts; DocRef and Shen et al. TKDE summaries
findings.strength: medium
findings.applies_at_this_size: Yes.

findings.claim: The modelling devices for the meaning layer are standard and cheap; their effect on agent tokens is untested and the nearby evidence on model-written or cached context is flat or negative.
findings.evidence: PROV-O (Entity, Activity, Agent; wasDerivedFrom, wasInvalidatedBy; qualified relations), Wikidata ranks (deprecated statements kept to stop re-adding known-wrong values), ADRs (numbered, never reused, superseded not edited; context, decision, status, consequences). Against: ETH AGENTS.md study cost +20-23% with -0.5% and -2% resolution; SWE Context Bench free summary reuse 22.22% vs 26.26% baseline; VibeMemBench 11 of 12 pairings no better than memory off, 160 of 231 failures in the form of the stored record. For: graphify-bench doc-and-code 80% vs 70% with Sonnet 5.
findings.source: W3C PROV-O, Wikidata help pages, Nygard 2011 (read); other lanes for the studies
findings.strength: strong as standards; medium for the effect studies
findings.applies_at_this_size: Yes; the model specifies the form of the record, which is where most measured failures were.

recommendations.what: R1. Write the schema as data derived from the 16 competency questions (each with type, stratification level, metapath, answer shape, token ceiling); script the forward check (every node and relation kind serves a question), the backward check (every question has a path) and counted constraint violations; prune candidates same_capability, migration_follows, mocks, contains/defines as edges, pairwise co_changed.
recommendations.from_theory: Gruninger and Fox via Uschold and Gruninger 1996 (stratified CQs, minimal sufficiency, completeness check, pruning rule); Noy and McGuinness; Keet and Khan 2024; HIN network schema (Shi et al.); Hogan 7.3.2 violations per constraint.
recommendations.expected_effect: No recall change by itself; a justified kind list, exposure of the five questions v1 cannot answer by type, a smaller schema; any token gain comes from smaller answers.
recommendations.how_to_test_on_tuning_data: Remove the pruning candidates and re-score tuning T1 and the 20 tuning TQ questions at equal answer size; a kind stays if tuning recall falls beyond the paired interval; if most pruned kinds are needed, the question list is incomplete.
recommendations.replaces_in_current_graph: A schema grown from extractor convenience and scored on one question family (co-change recall, CQ10, 1.8% of product carried tokens).

recommendations.what: R2. Metapath registry from the schema with a hop budget per relation, plus candidate extra metapaths discovered from tuning seed-target and co-change pairs.
recommendations.from_theory: HIN metapaths; Lao and Cohen path-constrained random walks (one weight per edge-label sequence); Meng et al. 2015 meta-path discovery from example pairs.
recommendations.expected_effect: Unknown; ranking effect belongs to the ranking lane. Risk of overfitting 65 tuning commits.
recommendations.how_to_test_on_tuning_data: Cross-validate inside the tuning set: registry paths against discovered paths at fixed answer size; reject if discovered paths do not beat the hand-set by more than the interval.
recommendations.replaces_in_current_graph: Hand-set traversal and a sweep of 60 hand-chosen configurations.
recommendations.verdict: Do after R1, coordinate with the ranking lane.

recommendations.what: R3. Model the change set as a ChangeSet node (sha, date, message, PR, size) with touches edges carrying role and hunk spans to files and definitions; weight a co-change step by w/|e| (hypergraph random walk) and keep the 30-entity cap, with sweep size as a property.
recommendations.from_theory: Zhou, Huang, Scholkopf 2006 (clique weight w(e)/delta(e), hypergraph random walk); ROSE (transactions, rules between entity sets, 30-entity cap); Fatemi et al. 2020 (star-to-clique loses information).
recommendations.expected_effect: Moderate on co-change recall if sweeps are noise, none if they carry signal; gives the first answer to the 'and why' of CQ10 and CQ6 through the message and PR. Direct token effect small (CQ10 is 1.8% of product carried tokens).
recommendations.how_to_test_on_tuning_data: Tuning commits, recall at the fixed 8,000-token answer for (a) v1 pairwise confidence, (b) pairwise weight 1/(k-1), (c) the hypergraph walk, stratified by seed commit size; no gain over (a) beyond the paired interval means the set model adds meaning but not ranking.
recommendations.replaces_in_current_graph: 1,896 pairwise co_changed edges with ROSE-style confidence and no commit nodes or messages.
recommendations.verdict: Do; about an hour of scripting.

recommendations.what: R4. Stable identity: entity key, occurrence and lineage separated. Keys: route = runtime plus method plus path template; table.column; setting, outbox kind and string-key literals; commit sha with patch-id across rebases; (document family, id) never reused; sections by explicit id or heading path with content hash, never line number; rules by an id written into the source (owner decision) or a minted id; definitions by minted opaque id with an alias table of SCIP-form qualified names. Lineage edges (renamed_from, moved_from, split_from, merged_into, candidate_of) from a deterministic ladder: git diff -M file map, exact qualified name, exact name and signature in another file, body similarity (about 0.8, tune), else created or deleted; uncertain matches mark anchors suspect, never silently re-point.
recommendations.from_theory: Hogan 3.2 persistent identifiers; git rename detection and patch-id; origin analysis (Godfrey and Zou); method-history tools (CodeShovel, CodeTracker, HistoryFinder); entity resolution blocking, matching, NIL; ADR numbering; PROV specializationOf and wasInvalidatedBy.
recommendations.expected_effect: None on structural retrieval over one snapshot; it is the precondition for any stored conclusion or citation check. Measured on v1: a quarter of section ids and half of URL-site ids gone within three weeks, some silently mis-bound.
recommendations.how_to_test_on_tuning_data: Orphan and mis-bound rate: treat cached snapshots as pseudo-claims anchored at snapshot S and count, at the frozen commit, anchors resolving by (a) id string, (b) natural key, (c) the ladder, (d) the wrong entity. Skip the body step if under 1% of anchors are orphaned by it beyond the name key (the v1 audit used the same 1% rule); mis-binding must be zero.
recommendations.needs_install: None (git, Python or Node already present). PyRef not recommended (precision 89.6% and recall 76.1% by its authors, F1 0.64 independent; summaries only).
recommendations.replaces_in_current_graph: Id-string identity including line-number section ids, ordinal invariant ids and line-number URL-site ids; the --no-renames git history.
recommendations.verdict: Do before any cached conclusion or citation check is stored.

recommendations.what: R5. The meaning layer as a model: Document, Section, Item, Rule, Decision, Claim, Evidence, Source; relations defines, cites (span, hash at citing, status), constrains (role: guard, client half, condition input, example, violation), justified_by, depends_on, supersedes, about, rests_on (with hash), refutes, supports, derived_from; computed statuses valid, suspect, superseded, unanchored; ambiguous(k) and not_in_repo as statuses; refuted claims kept with a deprecated rank. Deterministic extractor for ids, headings, citation spans with hashes and invariant anchors with hand-assigned roles for the 20 invariants; any model-read field fills the form and never creates a code edge unaided.
recommendations.from_theory: PROV-O qualified relations; Wikidata statements, references and ranks; ADR; competency-question stratification (CQ1, CQ2, CQ4, CQ9, CQ14); entity linking with NIL; Dagenais and Robillard; provenance semirings for the dependency-set idea.
recommendations.expected_effect: Largest candidate saving among the layers (document, rule and plan questions are 8.7%, 8.4% and more of product carried tokens, a larger share of program work; upper bounds from use-cases.md, not forecasts); effect evidence is mixed.

ranking.summary: At this size (about 5,000 nodes, 18,875 edge rows, 65 tuning commits) the principled ranker is small. Pool the candidates (2 typed hops plus co-change neighbours), then combine rooted PageRank with smoothed co-change evidence, by reciprocal-rank fusion or a ridge logistic regression refit on earlier commits only. A pilot on the 65 tuning commits (rolling origin, 50 test commits) showed these two signals carry nearly all the ordering power. Fusion beat PageRank alone by +0.030 P@10 (95% interval +0.015 to +0.044). A 25-feature logistic model matched a 2-feature one (+0.001, interval -0.007 to +0.009). A linear latent model added nothing (+0.001). Embeddings and GNNs are not justified at this size, by evidence and density arguments only. I trained no embedding or neural model, so the RotatE verdict is a prediction with a test specified, not a measurement. 'What breaks' needs directed dependents and outcome ground truth (failing tests from differential runs), not co-change labels. Everything recommended needs no install except the optional arms.

findings.claim: Simple proximity scores give large lifts over chance on co-authorship graphs of the same size as this one; sums over all paths (a Katz variant) often beat shortest path and common neighbours; even the best predictor was right only ~16% of the time.
findings.evidence: Five arXiv co-authorship graphs with 2,122 to 5,469 authors and 5,724 to 41,852 edges; time split (train 1994-96, test 1997-99); factors of 40 to 50 over a random predictor; on a narrow community (STOC/FOCS) no method beat random by more than about 7.
findings.source: Liben-Nowell and Kleinberg, JASIST 2007 (people.csail.mit.edu/dln/papers/link/paper.pdf, text extracted)
findings.strength: strong for direction; medium for numbers (one data family)
findings.applies_at_this_size: Same scale. The narrow-community result is the warning: one repository and one team is the hard case.

findings.claim: Among local indices RA is marginally best, CN and AA close behind; the differences exist only on networks with high clustering and high degree heterogeneity. Preferential attachment is at or below chance on physical networks. Sparse graphs produce severe score ties.
findings.evidence: Six networks (332 to 5,022 nodes), AUC with 90/10 random split, 10 repeats: RA 0.955 vs AA 0.925 on USAir, 0.931 vs 0.922 on political blogs; ties elsewhere. Survey: PA 0.446 on the power grid; on the router network CN gives 99.59% of pairs a zero score.
findings.source: Zhou, Lue, Zhang 2009 (arXiv 0901.0553); Lue and Zhou survey 2011 (arXiv 1010.0725), via ar5iv
findings.strength: medium
findings.applies_at_this_size: Yes. Pilot agrees: RA minus CN +0.012 P@10 [0.002, 0.022]; popular-first ordering scored 0.140 against 0.132 random.

findings.claim: Katz, rooted PageRank and SimRank can be approximated from the h-hop subgraph around a pair (walks up to length 2h+1 captured); a learned subgraph GNN (SEAL) beat the best heuristic on 7 of 8 graphs, but with random negatives, no node types, and 90% of edges as training positives.
findings.evidence: Eight graphs, 297 to 5,022 nodes, 2,126 to 16,714 edges. AUC examples: Power 76.15 to 87.61, Router 56.43 to 96.38, Yeast 92.76 to 97.91, USAir 95.77 to 96.62; PageRank tied SEAL on C.elegans (90.32 vs 90.30).
findings.source: Zhang and Chen, NeurIPS 2018 (arXiv 1802.09691, ar5iv)
findings.strength: medium (self-reported, random negatives)
findings.applies_at_this_size: Graph size matches; the supervised signal does not (thousands of positive edges there, 65 independent commits here).

findings.claim: Under hard, heuristic-selected negatives the margin of learned link predictors over heuristics shrinks or reverses on structure-dominated graphs, but not on feature-rich ones.
findings.evidence: Same tuning budget for all methods. ogbl-collab (235,868 nodes) MRR: Katz 6.31, RA 6.29 vs GCN 6.09, SAGE 5.53. ogbl-ppa: RA 28.34 vs SAGE 27.27, GCN 26.94. Cora: GAE 18.32 vs AA 11.91. Pubmed: SAGE 9.40 vs Katz 3.01.
findings.source: Li et al., NeurIPS Datasets 2023 (arXiv 2306.10453, html; last 22k of 122k chars unread)
findings.strength: medium to strong
findings.applies_at_this_size: Mixed; structure-dominated graph logic fits the code graph's structure, feature-rich logic fits its text.

findings.claim: Specialised heterogeneous GNNs are matched or beaten by plain GCN/GAT with proper inputs on link prediction.
findings.evidence: Amazon ROC-AUC: GCN 92.84, HGT 88.26, RGCN 86.34, Simple-HGN 93.40; LastFM: GCN 59.17, HGT 54.99, Simple-HGN 67.59; PubMed: GCN 80.48, HGT 80.12, Simple-HGN 83.39. Graphs have 10,099 to 63,109 nodes and 141,521 to 244,986 edges.
findings.source: Lv et al., KDD 2021 HGB benchmark (arXiv 2112.14936, ar5iv)
findings.strength: medium to strong
findings.applies_at_this_size: Heterogeneity-specific machinery rarely pays, and these sets have 8 to 13 times the edges of this graph.

findings.claim: Binary 'this typed path exists' features with a logistic classifier (SFE) match random-walk-probability features (PRA) and are much cheaper; hard negatives sampled by personalised PageRank similarity.
findings.evidence: MAP .344 vs .337 on Freebase and .319 vs .303 on NELL (p .55, .25); 10 NELL relations PRA .3704 in 44 min vs SFE-BFS .4799 in 5 min (p<0.05); abstract MAP .432 to .528. Logistic regression with elastic net tuned on a development split.
findings.source: Gardner and Mitchell, EMNLP 2015 (ACL anthology pdf, pdftotext)
findings.strength: medium
findings.applies_at_this_size: Yes, cheap; kind-sequence features are SFE features. At 65 commits the pilot's kind flags added +0.003 [-0.004, +0.011], below resolution.

findings.claim: A rule miner (AnyBURL) is competitive with or better than embeddings in about 1,000 s without tuning; an independent 16-model study calls it a very challenging baseline with only ComplEx-N3 comparable; embeddings do better where relational-path support is high.
findings.evidence: FB15k-237 H@1 27.34 vs RotatE 23.83, ComplEx 25.72, TuckER 25.90; WN18RR H@1 45.69 vs RotatE 42.60; Laplace smoothing pc=5; 272,115 / 86,835 training triples.
findings.source: Meilicke et al. (arXiv 2004.04412, ar5iv); Rossi et al., TKDD 2021 (arXiv 2002.00819, ar5iv)
findings.strength: medium (authors' own, partly copied baselines) plus medium to strong (independent study)
findings.applies_at_this_size: Good fit: fast on ~19k triples, outputs readable rules; the smoothing constant is worth copying even without the tool.

findings.claim: Reported embedding wins on FB15k, WN18 and YAGO3-10 are inflated by leakage and, for some neural models, by tie handling; tuned simple baselines match published models.
findings.evidence: 142 of 1,345 FB15k relations are Cartesian-product; a simple rule FHits@1 71.6% vs best embedding 73.8% (FB15k), 96.4% vs 94.6% (WN18), 51.6% on YAGO3-10 above every embedding; ConvE FMRR .698 to .305 after removing redundancy. ConvKB .396 reported vs .243 random ties; CapsE .523 vs .150. Tuned DistMult FB15k MRR .798 vs .35 original.
findings.source: Akrami et al. SIGMOD 2020 (arXiv 2003.08001); Sun et al. ACL 2020 (arXiv 1911.03903); Kadlec et al. (arXiv 1705.10744), all via ar5iv
findings.strength: strong for the leakage and tie claims
findings.applies_at_this_size: A warning about the baseline for any embedding arm: it must be tuned and its negatives and ties must be controlled.

findings.claim: Embedding quality depends on triples per entity; on sparse, noisy graphs embeddings fell below simple baselines.
findings.evidence: Half of FB15k triples removed at random (sparse) left TransE/TransH/HolE/STransE up to 60% worse Hits@10 than the same number removed by relation; on NELL165 they scored AUPRC .70 to .78 vs a threshold baseline .873 and a probabilistic model .891. Entity density: FB15K 79, FB15k-237 about 37, WN18 about 7, this graph 6.9 (measured here).
findings.source: Pujara, Augustine, Getoor, EMNLP 2017 (linqs.org pdf, pdftotext)
findings.strength: medium (one study, four 2013-2016 models)
findings.applies_at_this_size: This graph has 18,875 edge rows (14 times fewer triples than FB15k-237) and 388 tuning queries.

findings.claim: A no-learning memorisation baseline (EdgeBank, recency-decayed repeat count) is competitive with temporal GNNs and temporal KG models; rankings of methods change with the negative sampler.
findings.evidence: EdgeBank AP LastFM .79 vs TGN .72 (random negatives); best under historical negatives on UN Trade .73, UN Vote .71, Contact .77; the unlimited version collapses to about .5 under harder samples. Recurrency baseline MRR GDELT 24.5 vs 21.7 (TiRGN), ICEWS18 28.7 vs 33.7, ICEWS14 37.2 vs 47.4; first or third on 3 of 5 sets. TGB: EdgeBank beats DyRep and nearly matches TGN on tgbl-coin.
findings.source: Poursafaei et al. NeurIPS 2022 (arXiv 2207.10128); Huang et al. NeurIPS 2023 (arXiv 2307.01026); Gastinger et al. IJCAI 2024 (arXiv 2404.16726)
findings.strength: medium to strong
findings.applies_at_this_size: Co-change is an EdgeBank; the correct comparison for any temporal model here is windowed, decayed co-change.

findings.claim: Temporal rules (backward temporal walks, confidence plus exponential time decay, noisy-OR) beat temporal embeddings and recent neural models on temporal KG forecasting.
findings.evidence: ICEWS14 (63,685 training facts, 7,128 entities, 230 relations): MRR 0.4304 vs xERTE 0.4079, RE-Net 0.3828, CyGNet 0.3273, static AnyBURL 0.2967, TTransE 0.1343; rule learning 180 s on 8 CPUs; time term 0.5*confidence + 0.5*exp(-0.1*dt).
findings.source: Liu et al., TLogic, AAAI 2022 (arXiv 2112.08025, ar5iv)
findings.strength: medium
findings.applies_at_this_size: The recency term and noisy-OR are cheap to copy; the miner needs thousands of events per relation, this graph has about 230 commits.

findings.claim: Co-change mining needs history on the scale of tens of thousands of commits; very short histories are precise on the few queries they can answer; filtering transactions above 8 files helps; the strongest feature of a learned co-change ranker is the earlier co-change count and everything else adds a few percent.
findings.evidence: 2 industrial + 17 open-source systems, last 50,000 commits each, 660 sampled transactions per system: about 25,000 commits needed for applicability to level off; age zero best. Learning to rank on 150 Java projects (634,216 pull requests): permutation importance 0.3844 for co-change count vs 0.0539 path similarity, 0.0392 author similarity, 0.0082 code dependency; random forest best of 8 learners (LambdaMART included), NDCG@5 0.8394, +4.7% over plain support ranking.
findings.source: Moonen, Di Alesio, Rolfsnes, Binkley (Simula pdf, pdftotext); arXiv 2411.19099 (html, last 54k of 154k chars unread)
findings.strength: medium to strong (history length study); weak to medium (learning-to-rank study)
findings.applies_at_this_size: This repository has 233 non-merge commits (140 usable), about 0.5% of the sufficient history; co-change is sparse (36.1% of tuning seeds have no co-change candidate) and must be one signal among several.

findings.claim: The base rate for a learned model beating a tuned simple baseline is low in recommendation research, and selection on a small noisy estimate can overfit as much as the gap between algorithms.
findings.evidence: 18 deep-learning recommenders examined, 7 reproducible, 6 of 7 did not consistently beat tuned simple baselines, the 7th did not consistently beat a tuned linear method; some papers tuned epochs on test data. Cawley and Talbot: selection-bias overfitting can be as large as differences between algorithms (abstract). Random and leave-one-out splits leak the future (Ji et al.).
findings.source: Ferrari Dacrema et al. RecSys 2019 (arXiv 1907.06902); Cawley and Talbot JMLR 2010 (abstract only); Ji et al. (arXiv 2010.11060)
findings.strength: strong for the reproducibility count; medium for the rest
findings.applies_at_this_size: Direct: v1 tuned 60 configurations on 65 commits.

findings.claim: Pilot on this graph (tuning split only): PageRank and co-change carry almost all the ordering power; a fitted 25-feature combination is no better than a 2-feature one.
findings.evidence: 65 tuning commits (388 seeds, 2,924 seed-truth pairs, leak-free parent snapshots), rolling origin over the late 50 commits. P@10: random in pool 0.118, PPR 0.204, co-change 0.199, RRF(PPR, co-change) 0.233, 25-feature ridge logistic 0.232, 2-feature 0.231, oracle ordering of the pool 0.356. Paired: RRF minus PPR +0.030 [+0.015, +0.044]; 25-feature minus 2-feature +0.001 [-0.007, +0.009]; spectral rank-64 minus PPR -0.007 [-0.021, +0.006]; RRF with spectral minus RRF +0.001 [-0.005, +0.006]. Pool ceiling 71.3% of truth pairs at a mean of 46 candidates; 92.3% with 3 hops at a mean of 121.
findings.source: My own computation, scripts in scratchpad .../graph-v2-pilot-ranking/ (feat.py, ev.py, svd.py); data: facts cache and git log
findings.strength: medium (one repository, one month, 65 independent commits, no held-out touched; unresolvable below about 0.02 P@10)
findings.applies_at_this_size: Measured at exactly this size; effects under about 0.02 P@10 cannot be resolved with the tuning set.

recommendations.what: R1. Two-stage ranker. Stage 0: pool = code files within 2 hops on the file-collapsed typed graph plus all co-change neighbours (ceiling 71.3% of truth pairs, about 46 candidates). Stage 1: at most 8 features (rooted PageRank alpha 0.15, hop indicators, smoothed co-change confidence/support/recency, RA, same slice/runtime/test flag, direct-edge kind, lexical similarity). Stage 2: Arm F = reciprocal-rank fusion (k=60) of the PageRank rank and, where present, the co-change rank (no fitted parameter); Arm L = ridge logistic regression refit before each test commit on earlier commits only, kept for calibrated probabilities that a token-budget packer needs.
recommendations.from_theory: Path-sum link prediction (Liben-Nowell and Kleinberg; Zhang and Chen gamma-decaying theory), recurrence/EdgeBank baselines (Poursafaei; Gastinger), SFE's logistic classifier (Gardner and Mitchell), rank fusion.
recommendations.expected_effect: About +0.03 P@10 over PageRank alone and +0.02 over a floor of directory/slice/runtime/test flags (pilot, tuning, 95% intervals above zero); coverage-limited: only seeds with co-change history gain (+0.055 on the 208 of 308 late seeds that have it, nothing on the rest). Ordering headroom to an oracle is 0.12 P@10 (0.233 vs 0.356).
recommendations.how_to_test_on_tuning_data: Rolling origin on the 65 tuning commits (train on earlier commits, min 15), paired bootstrap over commits. Kill: if RRF minus PPR has an interval including zero on all 65, demote co-change to a tie-breaker; if Arm L minus Arm F includes zero (it did in the pilot) keep Arm F as default and Arm L only if the packer needs probabilities. Placebo shuffled-feature columns and a learning curve as overfit checks; declare the arm list in advance.
recommendations.needs_install: None. Plain code; numpy 2.3.5 already in the host Python (pilot used nothing else).
recommendations.replaces_in_current_graph: v1's hand-weighted fusions, degree-normalised spreading and the 60-configuration one-factor sweep.
recommendations.verdict: Build first. Strong enough support in the literature and in the pilot; effect is modest.

recommendations.what: R2. Rebuild co-change as the weighted projection of the file-commit bipartite graph: each commit passes one unit split among its files (resource allocation, 1/(files-1) weighting), skip commits above 8 files, Laplace-smooth confidence with pc around 5, and sweep the recency half-life.
recommendations.from_theory: Bipartite network projection / NBI (Zhou et al. 2007: hit rate at L=10 16.2% vs 14.1% user-CF vs 10.3% popularity on 85,250 MovieLens links); transaction-size filter and age effects (Moonen et al.); AnyBURL smoothing; TLogic and recurrency time decay.
recommendations.expected_effect: Unknown; it changes the order of the strongest single signal (0.208 P@10 alone). The literature suggests size filtering and age matter more than the exact formula.
recommendations.how_to_test_on_tuning_data: Co-change-only P@10 for 12 variants: confidence; smoothed confidence pc 0/2/5/10; size-weighted RA; size cap 8/15/30; half-life 14/30/60/120 days/none. Choose on an inner rolling split, report all 12; kill if none beats the extractor's confidence by a paired interval above zero.
recommendations.needs_install: None. Uses the extractor's attrs.commits plus commit sizes from git log.
recommendations.replaces_in_current_graph: The extractor's confidence, support and 30-day recency weight taken as given.
recommendations.verdict: Build; cheap and attacks the strongest signal.

recommendations.what: R3. Depth-3 second tier, ranked by the same score, that the agent requests explicitly.
recommendations.from_theory: Hop literature quoted by the first round (depth 1 helps, depth 2 can hurt, odds fall 0.47 to 0.55 per extra hop); measured ceiling here.
recommendations.expected_effect: Ceiling rises from 71.3% to 92.3% of truth pairs at the cost of about 75 more candidates.
recommendations.how_to_test_on_tuning_data: R@20 and token cost with and without the tier; kill if R@20 does not rise by at least 0.05.
recommendations.replaces_in_current_graph: v1's unbounded hops (median reach 3,633 of 5,464 nodes per v1-audit.md).

recommendations.what: R4. Add a lexical similarity feature (names, path tokens, symbols) and test it against the 4-feature model.
recommendations.from_theory: First and second rounds: the search component dominates traversal in LocAgent ablations; pre-registered small-model study credits lexical or embedding entry.
recommendations.expected_effect: Unknown; not measured in the pilot.
recommendations.how_to_test_on_tuning_data: Paired contrast with and without the feature over the late 50 commits.
recommendations.replaces_in_current_graph: Nothing; fills a missing signal.

recommendations.what: R5. Typed path features (SFE) with an elastic-net penalty, as the explanation layer first and a feature set second.
recommendations.from_theory: Gardner and Mitchell 2015; Lv et al. (heterogeneity machinery rarely pays); NBFNet theory (all path scores are instances of one algebra).
recommendations.expected_effect: Pilot: direct-kind flags +0.003 [-0.004, +0.011], below resolution at 65 commits.
recommendations.how_to_test_on_tuning_data: Add the top 30 length-2 kind-sequence indicators to Arm L; kill if the paired interval versus the 2-feature model contains zero; revisit at 300 usable commits.
recommendations.replaces_in_current_graph: The per-kind class weights and 0.5 confidence floor chosen by hand in v1.
recommendations.verdict: Trial for explanations; not a feature set yet.

recommendations.what: R6. Rule-mining arm: AnyBURL on the typed graph with co_changed as the target relation, fused with PageRank.
recommendations.from_theory: Rossi et al. 2021, Meilicke et al., TLogic.
recommendations.expected_effect: Close to the path-feature model; the value is readable rules and a cross-check of R5.
recommendations.how_to_test_on_tuning_data: Top-10 from maximum-aggregated rules fused with PageRank on the late 50; kill if the paired gain interval contains zero.
recommendations.needs_install: AnyBURL jar (BSD-3, Java; input is TSV triples; jar size and required Java version not stated on the page, not downloaded). Offline, laptop-scale. Owner decision.
recommendations.replaces_in_current_graph: Nothing; extra arm.

recommendations.what: R7. Embedding arm (ComplEx-N3 and RotatE) per rolling-origin parent or every tenth parent, pool-restricted, fused; only with a tuned, multi-seed setup on an inner rolling split.
recommendations.from_theory: Pujara (density), Rossi (path support), Kadlec and Akrami (tuned and leak-free baselines), Sun (ties). Prediction: no gain at this size; linear latent proxy gave +0.001.
recommendations.expected_effect: Likely none at 18,875 edge rows and 388 queries; owner's RotatE experience is on dense graphs, 14 times more triples.
recommendations.how_to_test_on_tuning_data: Paired interval of RRF with the embedding score minus RRF over the late 50 commits; kill if it contains zero. Do not run an untuned or single-seed version.
recommendations.needs_install: PyKEEN 1.11.1 (MIT, 730 kB wheel, includes RotatE, ComplEx, TransE) plus PyTorch (CPU wheel, size not checked), inside a Linux container, offline, no GPU needed at this size. Owner decision.
recommendations.replaces_in_current_graph: Nothing; extra arm.

recommendations.what: R8. A separate 'break' ranker on directed dependents (reverse imports, calls, route-client, table readers), depth 2, with edge-kind priors from differential test runs, evaluated on recall of failing tests, never against co-change truth.
recommendations.from_theory: Legunsen et al. (class-level static selection 29.4% of tests, 0.2% unsafe vs method-level 43.8%, 10.6% unsafe), Musco et al. (richer call graphs raise completeness, lower precision), Meta predictive test selection.
recommendations.expected_effect: Different list from 'changes together'; directed dependents saturate at about 8 files, 2% of the repository, against a quarter of it for the undirected closure (first-round measurement).
recommendations.how_to_test_on_tuning_data: Apply each commit's production diff to its parent, keep the parent's tests, run the suites; failing tests are truth. 89 of 141 usable commits are runnable with what is installed (feasibility lane). Laplace-smoothed share of edges per kind that carried a failing test gives the priors.
recommendations.needs_install: None beyond the containers and environments already on the host (Postgres 16 image for backend integration tests).
recommendations.replaces_in_current_graph: The single undirected change-reach list.
recommendations.verdict: Build the ground truth first; then the ranker.

recommendations.what: R9. Evaluation harness that cannot be fooled: rolling origin, commit-level bootstrap, paired contrasts, random tie-breaking with reported tie share, placebo feature columns, arm list declared in advance, learning curve, held-out touched once.
recommendations.from_theory: Ji et al. (random splits leak), Cerqueira et al. (repeated holdout over periods for non-stationary data), Cawley and Talbot (selection bias), Sun et al. (ties), Li et al. and Poursafaei et al. (negative sampling decides winners).
recommendations.expected_effect: Prevents false wins from selecting among 60 configurations on 65 commits; paired intervals are about +/-0.01 to +/-0.02 P@10, so effects under 0.02 are unresolvable.
recommendations.how_to_test_on_tuning_data: Re-score v1's final configuration and Arm F under the same harness; report all arms.
recommendations.replaces_in_current_graph: The one-factor-at-a-time 60-configuration sweep.

earlier_research_missed: First round ruled out trained graph models in one line ('Do NOT use ... trained graph models (CGM, GNN)') with no source; the evidence on small graphs exists and mostly agrees, for reasons of size and density rather than principle.

Neither round treated ranking as link prediction: no learning-to-rank, no feature-based fusion theory, no evidence on how much a fitted combination can be trusted with 45 to 65 independent commits; fusion weights (0.5, 1, 3) and PPR alpha were compared on the 45 test commits (critic.txt already flagged tuning on the test commits).

The first round quoted ~25,000 commits for co-change applicability (Moonen et al.) but did not draw the consequence: this repository has 233 non-merge commits (140 usable), about 0.5 percent of that, so co-change is sparse (36.1 percent of tuning seeds have no co-change candidate) and must be one signal among several; it also did not use the transaction-size filter above 8 files from the same study.
v1's primary metric (recall inside an 8,000-token answer) could not see ordering at 2 hops (graph-v2/v1-audit.md); no round fixed the list length to make ranking visible.

Link-prediction evaluation theory was missing: hard versus random negatives (HeaRT, EdgeBank), tie handling (Sun et al.: ConvKB .396 reported vs .243 random ties), future leakage from random splits (Ji et al.), selection bias (Cawley and Talbot).

Neither round separated 'what changes together' from 'what breaks' in ground truth and features; the second round also did not say how to avoid overfitting a model trained on its recommended rolling-origin splits.

Metapath similarity (PathSim, HeteSim), supervised path models (PRA, SFE, supervised random walks), rule mining (AMIE, AnyBURL), temporal rules (TLogic) and temporal baselines (EdgeBank, recurrency) were absent from both rounds.
could_not_verify: Did not train any knowledge-graph embedding, GNN, boosted-tree or rule-mining model; the verdicts on RotatE/ComplEx, GNNs and LambdaMART are predictions from the literature plus a linear spectral proxy, not measurements on this graph.

Not opened at all: original path ranking algorithm papers (Lao and Cohen 2010; Lao, Mitchell, Cohen 2011), AMIE and AMIE+ (only numbers quoted by Akrami), the RotatE paper, SimRank (Jeh and Widom), SZZ, Ying et al. 2004 and ROSE (first round read ROSE), TARMAQ itself (described via the history-length paper), Peduzzi's events-per-variable rule, Tax et al.'s learning-to-rank comparison.

Abstract, listing page or search summary only: Qin et al. (GBDT vs neural rankers), Cawley and Talbot, Cerqueira et al., Rolfsnes et al. 2018 (aggregation 13 to 90 percent), Liben-Nowell and Kleinberg's Katz factor table (the sentence naming how many sections Katz won was cut in my extraction).

Blocked: a temporal-graph-network study of change propagation (ScienceDirect, HTTP 403); the Simula paper on predicting relevance of change recommendations (bot check); the last 54k characters of the CoRanker paper (limitations), last 22k of the HeaRT paper, last 20k of the Lue-Zhou survey, last 8k of Akrami, appendix E of NBFNet.

Toutanova and Chen's observed-features results were not read in tables and rest on FB15K, which leaks (Akrami); AnyBURL's embedding baselines are partly copied from other papers; PathSim evidence is 15 labelled queries.
AnyBURL jar size and minimum Java version, and PyTorch's CPU wheel size, were not found; I downloaded nothing.

Pilot limits: one repository, one month, 65 independent commits, effects under about 0.02 P@10 unresolvable; the pool excludes the 29 percent of truth beyond 2 hops; P@10 at file level is not v1's token-budget recall so it cannot be compared with v1's 0.076 gap; alpha 0.15, Katz beta 0.1 and the 4 penalty values and 5 spectral ranks were the only parameters fixed or selected on these data; the extractor's co-change definitions (same-PR drop, 30-day half-life by hand) were taken as given; the canonical-loader edge count (about 16,500) was not reproduced (raw rows: 18,875).
No lexical-similarity, depth-3 ranking, symbol-level or token-budget ranking, or break ground truth was built or measured.

selection_interface.summary:
The selection and interface literature gives a principled answer builder and a small tool design for this graph, though almost all of the evidence comes from text and knowledge-graph question answering, not code agents. Full notes are in the notes file.

**What v1 does.** v1 fills each answer in rank order, with no per-item cost, no stopping rule, no redundancy control and no choice of detail level. This is the same rule as Aider's repository map.

**Selection, in the order I would build it:**
1. **Measured on the real graph (5,464 nodes, 16,462 edges, v1's own renderer and tokenizer).**
   - A symbol-signature line costs 33 tokens on average (spread/mean 0.4), so rank order is already near value-per-token order at that granularity.
   - A file-signature costs 156 tokens on average (spread 1.8, p99 1,446), and a snippet 270 per symbol (spread 2.9). At those granularities rank-prefix is a poor knapsack.
   - Median node degree is 4 (mean 6, p99 45, max 141), so plain one-hop lookups need no selection; selection matters for 2 to 3 hop impact sets, hubs and multi-seed questions.
2. **Cost-aware selection with a stop rule.**
   - Order items by calibrated relevance probability per token and stop when probability per token falls below 1/F. F is the tokens the agent would otherwise spend finding the omitted item (scripted search read about 695 per lookup in the first test).
   - This stop rule is my own derivation, not a published result. The knapsack and submodular guarantees behind it come from secondary sources.
   - An exact knapsack dynamic program is trivial at this size.
3. **Level of detail per node.** Choosing path, signature or snippet per node is a multiple-choice knapsack, and choosing a file or its symbols is a tree knapsack. This mapping is my inference, and I found no source applying it to code.
4. **Redundancy control.** Diversity packers show thin evidence. A 2026 submodular packer beat plain top-k by 0.051 F1 on one multi-hop set and was null on three others. MMR (a rule that penalises items similar to ones already picked) added 0.010 over naive packing in the same study.
5. **Connected-subgraph selection.** G-Retriever never ablated its Steiner step. SubgraphRAG got Hit 89.80 on WebQSP (GPT-4o) with plain top-100 triple scoring. An exact Steiner solver is feasible at this size, so no install is needed.
6. **Community summaries.** An independent evaluation found plain retrieval beat community global search on every detail benchmark. I do not recommend building summaries; the repository's slice, file and symbol hierarchy already exists.
7. **Format.** On the same facts in my measurement, a file-grouped tree is 0.43 times the token cost of triples and an adjacency list 0.61 times. JSON is 1.07 times and natural-language sentences 1.15 times. The accuracy evidence is weak: LocAgent's tree-versus-JSON comparison is 37 samples, and triples were not worse than prose in the one study that compared them.

**Interface:**
1. **Query language.** Do not give the model a query language. Strong models reach about 60 % execution accuracy on text-to-Cypher in CypherBench, and no model under 10B reached 20 %. CodexGraph lost on tokens (102k against 76k) and collapsed on a weak model.
2. **LLM-driven traversal.** It costs far more calls and tokens (Think-on-Graph 11.6 calls and 7,069 tokens per question, against 2 calls and 231 to 521 tokens for prepared-path designs).
3. **Fixed tools.** The recurring pattern is 3 to 4 fixed tools plus an exact-name and lexical entry point. LocAgent's ablation shows the entry point is worth 19 points of file accuracy and traversal about 2.
4. **Output limits.** The SWE-agent study shows summarised search beats step-through paging (18.0 % against 12.0 % resolved) and that a mid-sized output window beats both small and unbounded ones.
5. **Definition cost.** Every tool definition is paid on every call and every result stays in context. With the 31-versus-695 token lookup figures from earlier notes, three definitions of about 120 tokens (my assumption, not measured) over 40 calls break even at about 1.1 avoided searches. Four tools at the 950-token average Anthropic measured need about 11.
6. **Description wording.** Richer descriptions raised tool-selection and success but cost steps (+67 % steps, 16.67 % of cases worse in one study).
7. **Adoption.** Adoption must be measured per run: 58 % of CodeCompass trials made no graph call, and in the small-agent study the `find_entity` call rate fell from 96 % (14B) to 45 % (32B).

**What was not measured.** Nothing was run with a model, so how well a model reads the proposed formats on this repository is untested.

findings.claim: v1's selection is rank-prefix to a full budget, identical in kind to Aider's repository map, with no per-item cost, no stopping rule and no level-of-detail choice.
findings.evidence: packer.js: project() then pack() fills units in rank order, cuts the last unit, adds a footer, and a padding tail makes every arm's answer fill its budget. Aider repomap.py (read): PageRank-ranked definition lines fitted to a token budget by binary search with a 15 % tolerance; default 1,024 tokens, 8x when no files in chat.
findings.source: build/arms/common/packer.js; raw aider/repomap.py main
findings.strength: strong (code read)
findings.applies_at_this_size: Yes: this is the baseline that every selection recommendation is measured against.

findings.claim: Rank order is a poor knapsack at file and snippet granularity but nearly adequate at symbol-signature granularity, because item costs differ enormously only for the former.
findings.evidence: My measurement on the frozen graph (5,464 nodes, 16,462 edges), v1 tokenizer: symbol signature mean 33.3 tokens, CV 0.40, p90 50; file signatures mean 156.3, CV 1.80, p90 325, p99 1,446, max 2,950; symbol snippet mean 270, CV 2.87, max 18,329; whole file mean 2,218, CV 5.37. Path-only forms 13.5 to 18.2 tokens, CV 0.21 to 0.27.
findings.source: scratchpad/lane-sel-iface/fmt.js run read-only through build/arms/common loaders; notes section 2.1
findings.strength: strong for this graph (own measurement); approximate tokenizer
findings.applies_at_this_size: Yes, measured here. At 10x to 100x the size the per-item cost distribution is unchanged, so the conclusion holds.

findings.claim: At this graph size a one-hop neighbourhood is tiny; selection under a budget matters for 2 to 3 hop closure, hubs and multi-seed questions, not plain lookups.
findings.evidence: Degree over 5,462 connected nodes: mean 6, median 4, p90 12, p99 45, max 141. A median one-hop dump is about 4 edges, about 60 to 150 tokens depending on format.
findings.source: own measurement, notes section 2.2
findings.strength: strong for this graph
findings.applies_at_this_size: Yes. At 10x to 100x size with the same degree distribution one-hop stays small; two-hop closure grows roughly with degree squared.

findings.claim: Knapsack and submodular theory gives usable guarantees, but at this size the exact optimum of the modular case is cheap, so the approximation factors are a safety argument rather than a reason to choose an approximation.
findings.evidence: Budgeted maximum coverage 1-1/e (Khuller, Moss, Naor 1999; Sviridenko 2004: snippets/secondary); ratio greedy plus best singleton proven 0.405 and the older 1-1/sqrt(e) proof has a gap (arXiv 2008.05391 abstract page, read); CELF best-of-two (1-1/e)/2 with up to 700x speed-up (slides/snippets).
findings.source: arXiv 2008.05391; Khuller et al. IPL 70(1) 1999 and Leskovec et al. KDD 2007 via secondary sources; AdaGReS 2512.25052 and RCD 2605.00336 (read) restate the cardinality-case 1-1/e
findings.strength: strong theory, primary texts not opened in this session
findings.applies_at_this_size: Exact dynamic program over a few thousand items times 8,000 tokens is about 1e7 steps; no scale issue even at 100x.

findings.claim: The principled stop for 'smallest sufficient answer' is a value-density threshold: include item i only if p_i*F > c_i, so lambda = 1/F, which makes long budgets stop earlier than they fill.
findings.evidence: My derivation (decision-theoretic, modular case); illustration with F ~695 tokens (first test's scripted search, from earlier notes), symbol item ~33 tokens gives a break-even relevance of about 4.7 %; held-out precision at 10 items was about 0.26 to 0.28. Published relatives: Adaptive-k cuts at the largest similarity gap, about 99 % fewer input tokens than full context on 128k-token factoid QA (GPT-4o) and matches or beats fixed top-k (oracle k is optimistic); Sufficient Context autorater 93 % accurate on 115 labelled cases, models hallucinate 15 to 40 % with insufficient context.
findings.source: arXiv 2506.08479; arXiv 2411.06037 (both read); Cognition SWE-grep blog (vendor); derivation in notes section 3.3
findings.strength: medium for the published relatives, derivation untested; weak for the numeric illustration
findings.applies_at_this_size: Depends on calibration and on measuring F on the tuning commits; the rule has no scale dependence.

findings.claim: Evidence that diversity control or submodular packing beats a plain ranked list is thin, small and mostly on passage text.
findings.evidence: 2607.00725: HotpotQA, 160-token budget, 3B reader, 3 seeds: F1 packer 0.451, focused heuristic 0.429, MMR 0.410, naive top-k 0.400, LLMLingua-2 0.326; packer vs naive +0.051 (CI +0.030 to +0.072), vs heuristic +0.022; null on MuSiQue (-0.003), 2Wiki (+0.016), CovidQA (+0.010); vs heuristic -0.010 at 7B, -0.029 at 14B (p=0.013), +0.001 at 32B; authors say 1 of 14 contrasts positive and 1 negative is about chance. RCD: at 256 tokens plain Lead (0.242 ROUGE-1) beat MMR (0.141) and the submodular objective (0.138) on extractive MIMIC.
findings.source: arXiv 2607.00725 v2, 2605.00336, 2512.25052 (read); Carbonell and Goldstein SIGIR 1998 (abstract: modest benefit)
findings.strength: medium for the one positive on HotpotQA, weak beyond that; 2026 preprints not independently replicated
findings.applies_at_this_size: Redundancy in code answers is structural (symbol vs its file, test vs subject, slice siblings) and is better handled by hierarchy than by a similarity penalty; audit the share of repeated structure before building.

findings.claim: Choosing the level of detail per node (path, signature, file signatures, snippet) is a multiple-choice or tree knapsack with an exact dynamic program; this is where cost-aware selection should pay.
findings.evidence: Tree Knapsack Problem (selecting a node forces its ancestors) has an exact depth-first DP in time proportional to nodes x capacity (search snippets, INFORMS); multiple-choice tree knapsack used for level-of-detail simplification of graphics models (snippet). The mapping to file vs symbols vs snippets is my inference; no source applies it to code or LM context.
findings.source: search snippets of Johnson and Niemi 1983 and related tree-knapsack papers; notes section 3.5
findings.strength: strong old theory, application unproven
findings.applies_at_this_size: Yes: node and edge counts are tiny for the DP; the benefit depends on the cost spread measured in section 2.1.

findings.claim: LLM-written community summaries answer broad questions and lose detail; independent evaluation found plain retrieval equal or better on detail questions and matching at equal tokens.
findings.evidence: GraphRAG (2404.16130): context cost per level 2.6 % (root) to 73.5 % (lowest) of source text on a 1M-token corpus; win rate vs vector RAG 72 to 83 % comprehensiveness on global questions, LLM judged, no fact lookups. RAG vs GraphRAG (2502.11371): NQ F1 64.78 vs 54.48 (global), HotpotQA 60.04 vs 45.16, NovelQA 57.12 vs 39.17; token-matched plain retrieval 71.01 vs 71.17 for community-local on MultiHop-RAG (70B); construction 5,560 s vs 135 s.
findings.source: arXiv 2404.16130 and arXiv 2502.11371 v3 (read)
findings.strength: medium
findings.applies_at_this_size: This use case is specific lookups over a repository that already has a runtime/slice/file/symbol hierarchy; do not build summarisation. A 5k-node graph is below the size where community summaries were designed to pay.

findings.claim: Community detection choice (Louvain vs Leiden vs k-core) is a minor prior at this size; evidence is on text graphs.
findings.evidence: Louvain gave up to 25 % badly connected and 16 % disconnected communities in the Leiden paper's test networks and Leiden is proven to return connected ones; k-core GraphRAG paper (2603.05207): k-core variants won 70 to 75 % of judged comparisons with GPT-3.5-turbo but 45 to 55 % with GPT-5-mini, token sampler up to about 40 % fewer tokens, on graphs with average degree 2.88 to 4.42 and 55 to 60 % degree-1 nodes. This graph: median degree 4, mean 6, 10 % of nodes at degree 1.
findings.source: Traag, Waltman and van Eck 2019 (abstract via search); arXiv 2603.05207 (read)
findings.strength: medium for text corpora; none for code
findings.applies_at_this_size: Slice folders already give the grouping; expect small effect.

findings.claim: PCST/Steiner subgraph selection is not shown to beat simpler scoring; its evidence is retrieval-size reduction, and a bare tree can lose the answer.
findings.evidence: G-Retriever (2402.07630): prizes k-i for top-k by cosine, objective prize minus edge cost x C_e; k=3 nodes, k=5 edges, C_e=0.5 on WebQSP; 100,627 to 610 tokens (99 %); Table 6 has no remove-PCST row (without retrieval -9.43 %, without textualised graph -19.19 %, without graph encoder -22.51 %). SubgraphRAG (2410.20724): top-100 scored triples, one call, Hit 89.80 GPT-4o, 86.61 Llama 3.1 8B; random triples 60.14; weaker readers degrade with more triples. AGRAG (2511.05549): bare Steiner tree returned 'Tumors' where only the cyclic expansion got 'Blood vessels'; Steiner-only matched full method on fact retrieval and lost on summarisation. Ex-GraphRAG (2605.21994): PCST+top-25 +1.4 % single-hop, top-25 alone -9.8 % (-27.6 % with 3-hop).
findings.strength: medium to weak
findings.applies_at_this_size: Useful only for connection questions with 2 to 8 named terminals; exact Dreyfus-Wagner (about 3^k times polynomial) runs in milliseconds to seconds at 5,464 nodes; the 2-approximation (Goemans-Williamson; pcst_fast) matters only past about 10 to 12 terminals or at web scale.

findings.claim: Graph-fact format changes accuracy by a few points to tens of points on toy graphs and by about 10 points at most on the one code study; neighbour-grouped formats save 39 to 57 % of tokens on this graph.
findings.evidence: Own measurement on 64 symbol seeds (mean 12.8 edges), v1 tokenizer: triples 464 tokens (36.2/edge), JSON 495 (1.07x), sentences 532 (1.15x), adjacency 283 (0.61x), file-grouped tree 202 (0.43x). Accuracy: Talk like a Graph (2310.04560): encoding moved accuracy 4.8 to 61.8 points, incident/adjacency with integer ids best on counting; 2402.11541: shuffled triples beat fluent text, ordering effects 0 to about 5 points and model dependent, 90 % node replacement dropped ChatGPT from 54.0 to 19.8 on KQAPro; Lost in Serialization (2511.10234): cross-format SD 3.45 % (120B) to 10.5 % (fine-tuned 7B), shuffled edge lists hurt small fine-tuned models; LocAgent Table 9 (37 samples): file Acc@5 tree 79.41, JSON 76.47, incident 73.53; RepoGraph: 1-hop flattened 29.67 % at 2,311 tokens vs summarised 28.33 % at 718.
findings.strength: strong for token counts (own, approximate tokenizer); weak to medium for accuracy
findings.applies_at_this_size: Token ratios hold at any size; accuracy effect on a frontier agent on code is unmeasured.

findings.claim: Long answers cost more than their own tokens; position and length effects exist for older and open models.
findings.evidence: Lost in the Middle (2307.03172): GPT-3.5-Turbo with 20 passages 75.8 % first, 53.8 % middle (below 56.1 % closed-book), 63.2 % last. Length alone hurts (2510.05381): at 30,000 tokens Llama 3.1 8B fell 24.2 points on MMLU and 47.6 on HumanEval; GPT-4o about 7 on GSM8K. RCD: Lead minus Shuffled at most 0.017 ROUGE-1 at 256 tokens, 0.001 at 1,024 (GPT-4o).
findings.strength: strong for the 2023 models, medium for length alone; unverified for current frontier models
findings.applies_at_this_size: At answer sizes near 1,000 tokens harm from position is weak; put the highest-ranked items first at no cost.

findings.claim: Step-by-step LLM traversal of a knowledge graph is accurate but expensive; a small fixed set of read operations and good relation pruning are what matter, and beam width saturates early.
findings.evidence: ToG (2307.07697): up to 2ND+D+1 calls, N=D=3; LLM pruning beat BM25 and SentenceBERT (CWQ 58.8 vs 51.4/51.7; WebQSP 76.2 vs 58.7/66.3); width 3 to 5 gave 66.3 to 68.5; depth gains faded after 3. GCR (2410.13080) efficiency on WebQSP: ToG 75.1 Hit, 11.6 calls, 7,069 tokens; RoG 85.7, 2 calls, 521 tokens; GCR 92.6, 2 calls, 231 tokens; beam 10 best, 20 worse. RoG: without planning F1 49.69 vs 70.81. StructGPT (2305.09645): 74 % of sampled WebQSP failures were relation-selection errors. Graph-CoT (2404.07103): near-zero without demonstrations; GPT-4 46.28 vs LLaMA-2-13B 16.04. KG-Agent: 13 tools, no tool ablation.
findings.strength: medium; readers and metrics differ so the cross-paper cost comparison is not controlled
findings.applies_at_this_size: All are Freebase or Wikidata short-answer questions, none is code; the call-count lesson transfers, the accuracy numbers do not.

findings.claim: In code-agent evidence the lexical entry point matters far more than traversal, and the controlled studies of output size support summarised, capped, mid-sized output with no step-through paging.
findings.evidence: LocAgent ablation (7B ft; file Acc@5 / module Acc@10 / function Acc@10): full 88.32/82.85/71.53; no SearchEntity 68.98/61.31/53.28; no TraverseGraph 86.13/78.47/66.06; hops fixed at 1: 86.86/80.29/66.79; no BM25 75.18/68.98/60.22. SWE-agent (2405.15793) on SWE-bench Lite: summarised search 18.0 % vs iterative next-paging 12.0 % vs none 15.7 %; viewer window 100 lines 18.0 %, 30 lines 14.3 %, whole file 12.7 %; search returns at most 50 results and withholds the list above that. Small-agent study (2610.33958 v2): caps grep 40, read 80 default/120 max, find_entity 20, graph_neighbors 50 lines, every output 4,000 characters; exact-id scoring shrank the gain about 45 % (0.6B) and about 27 % (1.7B); no cap or ranking variation was tested.
findings.source: arXiv 2503.09089, 2405.15793, 2610.33958 v2 (read, tails partly unread)
findings.strength: medium (authors' systems; 2024 model for SWE-agent; Python only)
findings.applies_at_this_size: Transfers directly to a 5k-node graph; hop and output caps should be tuned on the tuning split.

findings.claim: Asking a model to write a graph query language adds a failure mode and cost that fixed tools avoid.
findings.evidence: CypherBench (2412.18702 v2): execution accuracy zero-shot Claude 3.5 Sonnet 61.58 %, GPT-4o 60.18 %, Qwen2.5-72B 41.87 %, Llama 3.1 8B 18.82 %, Llama 3.2 3B 11.20 %, no model under 10B above 20 %, on schemas of 7.5 relation types and 18.7 properties; common errors reversed direction and entity linking. CodexGraph (round 1): removing the Cypher-writing agent dropped CrossCodeEval exact match 27.90 to 8.30; 102.25k vs 76.01k tokens per SWE-bench sample; Qwen2-72B 1.95 % vs 9.34 %.
findings.source: arXiv 2412.18702 v2 (read, tail unread); arXiv 2408.03910 via round 1; Neo4j Text2Cypher benchmark (snippet only)
findings.strength: medium; 2024 models, entity-fact questions not code
findings.applies_at_this_size: This graph has 36 edge kinds; no study shows a frontier model reliably under 10 % error on such a schema.

findings.claim: Tool definitions are a standing per-call cost and their wording changes both selection and steps.
findings.evidence: Anthropic (advanced tool use, read): 58 tools across 5 servers about 55,000 tokens (about 950 per tool); 50+ tools about 77,000 tokens vs about 8,700 with on-demand search (stated 85 %, implied about 89 %); tool search accuracy 49 % to 74 % (Opus 4), 79.5 % to 88.1 % (Opus 4.5); use search above about 10 tools or 10,000 tokens; tool-use examples 72 % to 90 % on complex parameters. RAG-MCP (2505.03275): 13.62 % vs 43.13 % selection accuracy, prompt tokens down about 49 %. 2602.18914: selection probability +11.6 points functionality, +8.8 accuracy, +5.9 completeness, +1.5 conciseness (gpt-4o-mini, 10 servers); compliant description chosen 72 % vs 20 % baseline. 2602.14878: success +5.85 points median but steps +67.46 % and 16.67 % of cases worse; short variants equal, examples not significant.
findings.source: anthropic.com/engineering/advanced-tool-use and writing-tools-for-agents; arXiv 2505.03275, 2602.18914, 2602.14878 (read)
findings.strength: medium (vendor-internal and small benchmarks)
findings.applies_at_this_size: Three or four tools are far below the tool-search threshold; the lesson is to keep each definition short.

findings.claim: Reaching the tool is a precondition that must be measured per run.
findings.evidence: CodeCompass (round 2): 51 of 88 graph-available trials (58 %) made no graph call and averaged 80.2 % coverage vs 99.5 % for callers; small-agent study: find_entity called in 96 % of 14B episodes and 45 % of 32B episodes (round 1 figures); Hono replication (round 2): a control question never called the tool and one run silently never connected.
findings.source: earlier notes (research/lane-agent-graphs.txt, widen/lane-agents.md) re-cited; arXiv 2610.33958 v2 read for the tool set
findings.strength: weak to medium
findings.applies_at_this_size: Independent of graph size.

findings.claim: A tool definition of D tokens costs D*T tokens over a T-call task and a result of r tokens costs r*(T-t+1), so definition size and answer size are both multiplied by later calls.
findings.evidence: My arithmetic: one avoided scripted search saves about (695-31) x remaining calls, about 13,000 tokens at T=40; three tools of about 120 tokens (assumed) cost 14,400 over 40 calls, break-even about 1.1 avoided searches; four tools at 950 tokens cost 152,000 and need about 11. Cache reads were 96 to 98 % of baseline tokens in one published trace (round 2).
findings.source: derivation in notes section 4.5, inputs from widen/lane-agents.md
findings.strength: weak (derivation from other notes' numbers; definition token size not measured; depends on how the owner's metric counts cached input)
findings.applies_at_this_size: Independent of graph size; check in the pilot.

recommendations.what: Replace rank-prefix pack() with value-density selection and a cost-based stop. Order items by calibrated probability divided by rendered tokens; stop at the first item whose density is below lambda = 1/F, where F is the tokens the scripted baseline spends to locate one omitted relevant item, measured on the tuning commits; also stop at the cap B.
recommendations.from_theory: Knapsack (fractional greedy within one item of optimal; exact DP is cheap here); budgeted submodular selection with ratio greedy plus best singleton (0.405 proven, 2008.05391); Adaptive-k and Sufficient Context for stopping; precision-first scoring (SWE-grep); my decision-theoretic derivation of lambda = 1/F.
recommendations.replaces_in_current_graph: pack() in build/arms/common/packer.js: fill in rank order to the budget, with the padding tail that makes every answer fill its budget.
recommendations.expected_effect: Shorter answers at the same recall, mainly at file-signature and snippet granularity where item cost spread is 1.8 to 5.4; little change at symbol-signature granularity (spread 0.4). Illustrative break-even relevance near 5 % at 33 tokens per item if F is about 700 tokens. Smaller answers are also paid again on every later call (section 4.5).
recommendations.how_to_test_on_tuning_data: Same ranker, same facts: compare rank-prefix, density order and density order plus stop on the tuning split (65 commits, 388 T1 seeds) as recall-versus-tokens curves at 2k, 4k, 8k, 16k, tokens to 80 % recall and area under the curve; paired per commit; tune lambda on a grid around 1/F. Drop it if the curve does not move at any granularity. Power caution: paired SD of recall differences was 0.263 per commit, so 65 commits resolve only about 0.065; paired tokens-at-equal-recall should be tighter but is unmeasured. Remove the padding tail from this comparison or compare curves, not equal-size points.
recommendations.needs_install: None (Node, existing harness; exact knapsack DP is a few hundred lines).
recommendations.verdict: adopt as the first selection test

recommendations.what: Calibrate ranker scores into probabilities p_i (isotonic or Platt) fitted on tuning commits, so that the density and stop rules above have meaning.
recommendations.from_theory: The expected-value argument needs a probability; link-prediction and learning-to-rank lane is the source of the scores; calibration is the standard bridge.
recommendations.replaces_in_current_graph: Raw scores (PPR mass, fused scores) that are only ordinal.
recommendations.expected_effect: Makes the stop rule and cross-granularity comparisons possible; no effect on ranking order by itself.
recommendations.how_to_test_on_tuning_data: Reliability curve: bin scores on tune commits, compare predicted to observed hit rate; Brier score before and after on held-out folds of the tune split (no use of the held-out set).
recommendations.needs_install: None by hand (pool-adjacent-violators); or scikit-learn (about 30 MB, offline on Linux) in the existing Python.

recommendations.what: Choose one representation per node under the budget (path only, one signature line, file signature group, snippet) by multiple-choice knapsack, with the ancestor rule that a symbol line is not shown when a file form already contains it (tree knapsack).
recommendations.from_theory: Multiple-choice and tree knapsack dynamic programs (old theory; level-of-detail selection analogue in graphics); my mapping to code is an inference.
recommendations.replaces_in_current_graph: A fixed global output form (paths, signature, range or snippet) and granularity chosen per whole configuration.
recommendations.expected_effect: Largest gain where costs spread widely (file signatures p90 325 tokens, p99 1,446). Could let more distinct relevant items fit in the same tokens by using path-only for low-probability items and signatures for high-probability ones.
recommendations.how_to_test_on_tuning_data: Estimate q_r (the chance a representation spares the agent a follow-up read) from tune data, for example whether the item's own signature or line range sufficed to locate the edit; run the DP and compare recall per token against the best single fixed form at each budget; also a sweep of q_r over a small grid to show sensitivity.
