storage.summary: At this size (5,460 nodes, 17,370 typed edges) none of the storage and speed ideas changes anything an agent would notice in seconds or tokens. A whole-graph search over plain arrays takes about 80 microseconds (local, median over 514 files); a two-hop neighbourhood about 1 microsecond; a 40-iteration PageRank about 1.6 ms. The slowest measured engine query (about 270 ms) is about 4 percent of one 6.6 s model step. Arrays beat a SQLite recursive query by 28x to 148x on bounded hops (0.2 to 116 microseconds against 6 microseconds to 17 ms), which is a large factor on negligible absolute time. The 10 to 1,000 times larger engine figures are per-call overhead and application code (the SQLite arm ran about 270 statements per ranking), not graph storage. Reachability and distance indexes (closure, GRAIL, pruned landmark labelling) are point-to-point structures; the agent's questions are single-source, where one search is optimal (asking the labels for all targets is 40x slower than the search). Interval or prefix labels for containment are already present in the path-based ids. Reordering and compression save 45 KB of 65 KB. Rebuilding every index from scratch takes 25 ms median against about 5.3 s to extract a commit. Storage does not change answer size in tokens: the three engines returned identical answers; size is set by selection (median two-hop ball 110 nodes), what is returned per node, and serialisation (grouping identifiers by directory halves identifier text, an estimate). The one storage-related risk found is identity: 736 of 2,179 vanished node ids (34 percent) are line-number address changes that would falsely invalidate cached conclusions; history stored as validity intervals is 71x smaller than a copy per commit. Two decisions are worth making now: stable ids with file ownership and validity intervals on every fact, and one in-process call per question over arrays loaded from the fact table. Crossovers from the literature and a synthetic scale test: engine-level traversal differences from about 10^5 nodes with large frontiers, point-query indexes from 10^5 to 10^6 nodes, closure matrix infeasible between 55k and 546k nodes, reordering only when the working set is far beyond a 25 MB cache (hundreds of millions of edges).

findings.claim: Bounded graph traversal on this graph costs microseconds in plain arrays; a SQLite recursive query is 28x to 148x slower but still at most 17 ms; the gap grows with the number of edges touched.
findings.evidence: Frozen snapshot, 514 file-node sources, undirected all 36 edge kinds, zero answer mismatches: k=1 0.2 us vs 6 us; k=2 0.7 vs 45 us; k=3 5.2 us vs 484 us; k=4 28 us vs 2.9 ms; k=6 116 us vs 17.2 ms. Whole-graph search median about 80 us. Round 1's 10k to 1M node test: 29x, 23x, 18x at 6 hops.
findings.source: Local scripts exp1.js and exp8.js (scratchpad st/); round 1 lane-engines.txt local bench
findings.strength: medium (own code, one graph, warm, JavaScript)
findings.applies_at_this_size: Real but invisible: worst case is 0.26 percent of one model step.

findings.claim: The 0.3 ms to 270 ms engine timings are per-call overhead and application code, not graph storage.
findings.evidence: A 40-iteration whole-graph power iteration in typed arrays: median 1.64 ms (p90 1.93, max 3.13), 2.84 ms with a top-20 sort. Engine arms: 14.5 to 98.7 ms for the selected ranking; SQLite ran about 270 statements per ranking (256 ms); question lookups 0.3, 1.9 and 9 ms. Audit lists 'graph engines are faster than SQL' among claims not to make.
findings.source: build-f/engines_checked.json; local exp5.js
findings.strength: medium
findings.applies_at_this_size: Yes: the lever is number of calls and cold start (LadybugDB facts load 90 to 180 ms), not the engine.

findings.claim: Published engine comparisons split by implementation of the weaker arm and by scale, not by graph versus relational; folklore speedups are contradicted by indexed relational runs.
findings.evidence: Hohenstein and Jergler (500,000 nodes, 50 edges each, 5-way self-join): no index 59.7 s warm, with index 4.5 s (13x); cites a 2015 comparison where MySQL was about 6x faster than Neo4j at 5 hops. Vicknair et al. (1k to 100k node DAGs): Neo4j faster 'sometimes by a factor of 10' against an application-driven BFS issuing one SELECT per node; Neo4j store 1.25 to 2x larger. Lissandrini et al. (up to 76M nodes, 314M edges): relational-backed Sqlg significantly worse on traversal, BFS, shortest path, best on 1 to 2 hop label-filtered queries. Pacaci 2017 (round 1): PostgreSQL 11 GB vs Neo4j 20 GB at SF3.
findings.source: Hohenstein and Jergler DATA 2019; Vicknair et al. ACMSE 2010; Lissandrini et al. PVLDB 12(4) 2018; round 1 lane-engines.txt
findings.strength: medium (conflicting studies); weak for the Neo4j in Action claim, not opened
findings.applies_at_this_size: At this size every published difference is milliseconds; no source tests a code-shaped graph or agent tokens.

findings.claim: Point-to-point reachability and distance indexes (closure, GRAIL, pruned landmark labelling) do not serve single-source ranking and save microseconds here.
findings.evidence: Dependency subgraph is acyclic: closure 110,086 pairs (0.4 percent of n squared), 3.6 MB bit matrix, 3.5 ms build; GRAIL labels answer 83.4 to 95.5 percent of 'no' pairs (d=1..5) but BFS with early exit is 0.4 us; PLL 35 entries per vertex, 935 KB (6.5x the graph), query 0.65 us vs 41 us BFS; asking PLL for all 5,460 targets costs 3.5 ms vs 0.08 ms for one BFS. PLL paper: smallest graph 63k nodes, BFS 3.2 ms vs 0.5 us query. GRAIL authors: DFS 'quite attractive' on small datasets. Survey: partial indexes preferred because most queries answer no; dynamic partial indexes an open challenge.
findings.source: Akiba, Iwata, Yoshida SIGMOD 2013 (arXiv 1304.4661); Yildirim et al. PVLDB 2010; Zhang, Bonifati, Ozsu arXiv 2311.03542v2; local exp1.js
findings.strength: medium (authors' own experiments plus local)
findings.applies_at_this_size: No benefit. Crossover about 10^5 to 10^6 nodes with high point-query volume; closure bit matrix is 4 MB at 5.5k nodes, 355 MB at 55k, 35.5 GB at 546k.

findings.claim: Containment ('is inside', 'ancestor of') is already encoded by the path in the node id; interval labels add nothing at this size.
findings.evidence: 5,399 of 5,460 nodes carry a path; path tree 646 vertices, depth 6. Ancestor test 8.1 ns with pre/post integers vs 16.6 ns with a path-prefix compare, results agree. Theory: pre/post labels give constant-time descendant tests (XPath accelerator); SQLite uses an index for prefix patterns only with BINARY collation and GLOB (or case_sensitive_like).
findings.source: Grust, van Keulen, Teubner TODS preprint 2003; Agrawal et al. 1989 (abstract only); PostgreSQL ltree docs and SQLite optimiser docs (summary-level); local exp2.js
findings.strength: medium for theory, weak for the two documentation items
findings.applies_at_this_size: No benefit; matters only for relational ancestor queries over tens of thousands of tree nodes.

findings.claim: Reordering and compression matter only when the adjacency exceeds the processor cache; here the whole forward adjacency is 65 KB and path order is the natural good ordering.
findings.evidence: Local gap-coded bits per arc: path-and-line order 9.66, extractor order 10.39, random 18.21, reverse Cuthill-McKee 11.65, degree order 14.18, plain 32. Faldu et al.: 16.8 percent average speed-up on 18M to 64M vertices, 172M to 2.1B edges, 25 MB cache, 9 to 230 MB hot-vertex footprint; reordering can destroy community structure. WebGraph: 3.08 bits per link on 118M pages, 1B links, via URL order. This graph is less skewed than web graphs: 28 percent of vertices hold 67 percent of edge endpoints vs 9 to 26 percent holding 80 to 94 percent.
findings.source: Boldi and Vigna WWW 2004; Faldu, Diamond, Grot IISWC 2019 (arXiv 2001.08448); Balaji and Lucia IISWC 2018 (slides only); local exp2.js, exp10.js
findings.strength: medium
findings.applies_at_this_size: No. A graph 100x larger (14.6 MB adjacency) still fits in a desktop last-level cache; effects start near 10^7 or more nodes.

findings.claim: Caching traversals has nothing to save; rebuilding all indexes from scratch is negligible next to extracting the facts.
findings.evidence: Over 190 cached snapshots, full rebuild of three adjacency structures, components, closure, GRAIL and PLL: median 25 ms (p90 45, max 61) vs about 5.3 s to extract one commit. Per commit edges added median 60 (p90 388), removed median 3 (p90 67), about 0.9 percent churn. Hanauer et al. found dynamic algorithms beat static BFS/DFS even with caching on their instances; earlier all-pairs studies up to 700 vertices found the opposite.
findings.source: Local exp3.js; widen/critique-assumptions.md line 156 for the 5.3 s; Hanauer, Henzinger, Schulz ALENEX 2020 (arXiv 1905.01216); Gupta et al. 1993 and Mokhov et al. (abstract level)
findings.strength: medium
findings.applies_at_this_size: Incremental index maintenance is not needed. The token-relevant cache is of model-produced conclusions, via ownership and dependency sets (Glean model), not traversal results.

findings.claim: History as validity intervals is 71x smaller than a copy per commit, and a third of node-id churn is line-number identity breaks.
findings.evidence: 190 snapshots: 1,737,146 edge records if each snapshot is stored in full; 21,748 distinct typed edges; 24,579 validity intervals (about 20 MB vs 0.5 MB at assumed 12 and 20 bytes per record). Of 2,179 node ids that vanished between consecutive snapshots, 736 embed a line number (sec:<path>#L<line>, urlsite:<path>:<line>:...) and a node with the same kind, path and name appears in the same step (upper bound). Glean assigns facts to ownership units, recommending one per file.
findings.source: Local exp6.js and exp7.js; Glean incrementality documentation
findings.strength: medium (one repository, ordering by commit time not parent links)
findings.applies_at_this_size: Snapshots at 20 MB are still affordable; the identity problem is a correctness cost now.

findings.claim: Spatial topology for code has four concrete representations, all tiny.
findings.evidence: Containment: 646 path vertices, 105 directories, depth 6. Quotient on (runtime, slice): 58 super-nodes; 569 distinct links over all kinds, 172 over dependency kinds; 31.3 percent of all edges and 29.3 percent of dependency edges cross a slice, 11.2 and 1.6 percent cross a runtime; dependency map as text is 38 lines, 3,243 characters (about 800 to 1,100 tokens, estimate). Cross-runtime kinds: calls_url 91 percent of 77, constrains 100 percent of 85, same_capability 100 percent of 24, cites 82 percent of 496. Dependency-kind subgraph is acyclic and shallow (median reach 5, p90 38, max 454) because calls run file to symbol; all-kinds undirected reaches half the graph by 4 hops (median 2,752) and nearly all by 6.
findings.source: Local exp2.js and exp1.js on the frozen snapshot
findings.strength: medium (one snapshot)
findings.applies_at_this_size: Yes; this is the structure the agent can use.

findings.claim: Storage does not change answer size in tokens; selection, per-node content and serialisation do.
findings.evidence: Three engines gave identical ranked answers on every seed (audit). Two-hop ball: median 110 members (p90 405). Identifiers as one full id per line: median 5,404 characters (about 1,350 to 1,800 tokens at 3 to 4 characters per token, estimate); grouped by path 4,180; front-coded by directory 2,876 (median ratio 0.51). Per-node token field summed over the ball: median about 146,000 tokens (double counts file and symbols). Adjacency is 2 percent of exported bytes. Text encoding of graphs affects LLM accuracy (4.8 to 61.8 percent by task per Fatemi et al. abstract).
findings.source: build-f/engines_checked.json; local exp2.js; Fatemi, Halcrow, Perozzi arXiv 2310.04560 (abstract only); Lost in Serialization arXiv 2511.10234 (abstract only)
findings.strength: medium for the local counts, weak for the token estimates (no tokenizer offline) and the accuracy effect
findings.applies_at_this_size: Yes.

recommendations.what: Stable fact identity, file ownership and validity intervals: ids from kind, path and name with line numbers as attributes; an owner file on every node and edge; valid_from and valid_to commits instead of a copy per commit; every cached conclusion records the facts it read.
recommendations.from_theory: Glean ownership units and visibility rules; early cutoff from build systems; validity-interval encoding from temporal databases.
recommendations.expected_effect: Removes up to 736 of 2,179 spurious id vanishings over 189 steps (34 percent of id churn) and the false invalidations they cause; reduces 1.74M edge records to about 25k. No token effect on a fresh answer; it lets a cached conclusion survive an unrelated commit.
recommendations.how_to_test_on_tuning_data: Replay the 190 snapshots and count conclusions invalidated per commit under current ids, stable ids and file-hash keys. Fails if stable ids do not cut invalidations by about a third, or if more than a few percent of stable keys collide inside a file.
recommendations.replaces_in_current_graph: Line-number-bearing ids (sec:...#L<line>, urlsite:...:<line>:...) and the snapshot-per-commit store keyed by commit.

recommendations.what: One in-process call per agent question over typed arrays loaded from the fact table (forward and reverse, grouped by edge kind, about 0.15 MB, 4 ms median build); keep SQLite or Postgres as system of record with covering indexes on (kind, src, dst) and (kind, dst, src).
recommendations.from_theory: CSR or index-free adjacency gives a constant factor on traversal (28x to 148x here); per-statement overhead dominates small queries; GRainDB showed the factor comes from the access path, not the product category.
recommendations.expected_effect: Per-ranking time from 14.5 to 98.7 ms (engine arms) to the order of 2 to 3 ms for a comparable pass; avoids LadybugDB's 90 to 180 ms cold load; no token effect. Justified by simplicity, not speed.
recommendations.how_to_test_on_tuning_data: Add a typed-array arm to the existing interleaved engine bench on the tuning seeds; require identical ranked answers on all 200 seeds; drop it if not at least 5x faster than the best engine arm on the frozen primary; the agent test decides whether any latency is visible.
recommendations.needs_install: Nothing (plain typed arrays in Node, or numpy in the Python already on the host).
recommendations.verdict: adopt as implementation detail only if the agent harness pays for per-call latency; otherwise no change
recommendations.replaces_in_current_graph: Rankings run as many statements to an engine; the three-engine comparison as a research axis.

recommendations.what: Containment-aware answer format: write any node list as directory, then file, then symbols; group architecture-map answers by slice.
recommendations.from_theory: WebGraph locality and front coding of sorted keys with the containment tree as dictionary; graph text encoding affects model performance (Fatemi et al.).
recommendations.expected_effect: About 49 percent fewer identifier characters (median ratio 0.51 over 514 two-hop balls); estimated 1,350 to 1,800 tokens down to 720 to 960 for a median ball.
recommendations.how_to_test_on_tuning_data: Re-serialise the tuning answers in three formats and count tokens with the real tokenizer; then run the same agent tasks per format. Fails if real-token saving is under 20 percent or accuracy drops by more than agent-test noise.
recommendations.replaces_in_current_graph: One full id per line in answers.

recommendations.what: Materialise the slice and runtime quotient (58 super-nodes, 172 dependency links) as a per-commit GROUP BY view for use as an architecture map.
recommendations.from_theory: Graph summarisation by quotient; the repository's import-linter contracts as a partial order on slices.
recommendations.expected_effect: A whole-repository dependency map in about 800 to 1,100 tokens (estimate); whether it reduces agent search tokens is untested.
recommendations.how_to_test_on_tuning_data: Same tasks with and without the map; fails if search tokens do not fall. Coordinate with the summary-based retrieval lane.
recommendations.replaces_in_current_graph: Nothing; new view adjacent to the Louvain prior.

recommendations.what: Do not build transitive-closure tables, GRAIL labels, pruned landmark labelling, vertex reordering, graph compression, incremental index maintenance or a graph database for speed.
recommendations.from_theory: Point-to-point and all-pairs indexes do not serve single-source ranking; PLL's smallest case is 63k nodes; GRAIL authors call DFS attractive on small graphs; reordering gains need working sets far beyond a 25 MB cache; static recomputation is competitive at small size.
recommendations.expected_effect: Saves microseconds against a 25 ms full-rebuild budget and a 5.3 s extraction; avoids index code to maintain.
recommendations.how_to_test_on_tuning_data: Re-open only when nodes pass about 10^5 and a question needs thousands of point queries, or a six-hop query is needed on a million-node graph; then time the bounded query against its index on the larger repository.
recommendations.needs_install: Nothing recommended. If ever needed: LadybugDB (MIT, 5.8 MB wheel), DuckDB 2.0 with DuckPGQ (15.4 MB wheel, runs offline in a Linux container), Neo4j (GPL, JVM, about 380 MB image); all unnecessary at this size.
recommendations.replaces_in_current_graph: Round 1's suggestion to precompute closure or 'dependents within k' tables for hot files and to rank engines on latency.

earlier_research_missed: Round 1 treated storage as a speed contest and never connected speed to the agent's seconds or tokens; its own rule that latency under about 10 ms is irrelevant against a 6.6 s model step already implies the answer, but it still recommended precomputed closure or dependents tables for hot files, which is worth nothing here (dependency-subgraph closure is 110k pairs; a search over it is 0.1 microseconds).

Round 1 did not cover reachability and distance indexes, interval or prefix labelling of hierarchies, reordering and compression, validity-interval storage of history, or identity stability. This lane found the largest storage-related risk is identity: 34 percent of vanished node ids are line-number address changes.

Round 1 reported that a covering-index recursive query is as fast as its CSR for 1 to 3 hops; on the real graph arrays are 28x to 93x faster at those depths. The likely cause is its CSR baseline allocating an O(N) array per query (its own caveat), plus the graph's hubs (3-hop reach median 786); in absolute time the SQL query is 0.5 ms at three hops either way.
Round 1 left the Joern precedent at snippet level; the Joern page I opened gives no reason for the migration, so it stays snippet level.

The second round's 'a cache over traversal has nothing to save' is confirmed for traversal (25 ms full rebuild vs 5.3 s extraction), but its storage corollary was not drawn: ownership by file and stable ids are what make cached conclusions safe, and the line-number id problem was not seen.

Neither round noted that v1's calls edges run from a file to a symbol, so the dependency-kind subgraph is acyclic and shallow (median reach 5) while the all-kinds graph reaches nearly everything by 6 hops; this is a schema matter for the schema lane but it determines why ranking, not traversal, is the problem.
could_not_verify: Full text of Agrawal, Borgida, Jagadish 1989; Dietz 1982; GRIPP; BFL (cited only through the 2025 survey); ORDPATH; DeltaGraph; differential dataflow; Gupta et al. 1993 and Mokhov et al. (abstract level only); the Neo4j in Action benchmark (only second-hand via Hohenstein and Jergler).
Pacaci 2017, Kuzu CIDR 2023 and GRainDB are quoted from round 1 (lane-engines.txt) without re-reading.

Balaji and Lucia's IISWC 2018 paper: only the slides were opened. Hanauer et al.: conclusions read, instance sizes not. Fatemi et al., Lost in Serialization and GraphOmni: abstracts only. Glean: documentation page without timings. SQLite optimiser page and PostgreSQL ltree docs: summarising fetch or search summary only.

The pruned landmark labelling results table is scrambled in text extraction; I used only unambiguous values (query 0.5 to 16 us, BFS 3.2 ms to 1.5 s, smallest dataset 63k nodes and 148k edges, preprocessing up to 15,164 s, index up to about 22 GB).

All token figures derived from characters are estimates at 3 to 4 characters per token; no tokenizer is available offline. Per-node 'tokens' fields come from the project's export, method not re-derived.

My timings are one process on one machine in JavaScript, undirected projection, warm, host not quiet, single pass: orders of magnitude, not exact ratios. My loader gives 5,460 nodes and 17,370 distinct typed edges while the engine audit used 5,464 and 16,462; not reconciled. A 3-million-node synthetic run failed (set size limit) and was not retried; the synthetic graph is preferential attachment, not code-shaped.

Stability of cross-slice shares across commits (one snapshot measured); the 190-snapshot analysis orders by commit time, not parent links, so merges could pair non-parent snapshots; the identity-break count is an upper bound because names are not always unique.

I did not read round 2's design and protocol documents in full (only critique-assumptions.md by keyword) nor inspect the LadybugDB arm's code, so I make no claim about why its PageRank configuration is about 10x slower than my array loop.

a.summary:
I checked 36 design-deciding claims from the construction, modelling and storage lanes against their primary sources: paper PDFs extracted locally, arXiv HTML, official docs, source code and npm/PyPI metadata. I also re-counted the lanes' local numbers from the frozen-commit facts. Most literature claims hold as quoted.

Corrections that change a design decision:
(1) ROSE's 30-entity cap was a filter for CVS branch-merge transactions, not a tuned sweep-noise threshold. Its 64% top-three figure is at entity level; at file level it is 70%, with 26% recall.
(2) HistoryFinder's numbers are Java-only and scored on the authors' own oracle. The tool uses 70%/75% body-similarity thresholds, so a local sweep should start there, not at 0.8.
(3) Legunsen's 0.2%/33.0% and 10.6%/55.7% figures are shares of revisions with any violation, not shares of tests missed. The same paper says suites shorter than about 5 s should simply run all tests.
(4) Jelly evaluated no React, JSX or React Native code.
(5) The construction lane's '39 test_calls_route edges' is wrong. The frozen commit has 441 records: 382 test-route pairs, from 274 tests to 83 routes. This shrinks the gap that dynamic test edges would fill.
(6) coverage.py contexts record lines, not calls, and coverage.py is not a backend dependency.
(7) FastAPI's APIRoute internals are being refactored at master, and the backend's FastAPI version is unpinned (>=0.115,<1.0).
(8) Four different edge totals are in circulation. The true counts are 36 kinds, 18,875 records and 17,410 distinct typed edges.

Strongest support for the storage verdict: the GRAIL authors call plain DFS 'quite attractive' on their small datasets, which have 3.6k–39k nodes, the same order as this graph. CodexGraph confirms that a graph interface cost 7–15x the tokens of BM25 for equal or slightly better results; that should be the default expectation for any graph arm.

checks.claim: PyCG holds 49% of dynamic edges, 48.5% of callees; 59% of missing callees are built-in-type methods; ~12% name resolution; 95% callers; 39/50 projects (6 timeout, 3 OOM, 2 crash)
checks.corrected: All figures verbatim. The data is 50 Python projects (~681k lines of code, 30k tests), with the dynamic graph taken by DynaPyt at 215 min per project. The figures describe PyCG, not v1.
checks.source: DyPyBench, Proc. ACM SE 1 FSE 2024, arXiv 2403.00539 HTML

checks.corrected: 6 applications. In A.W. mode PyCG recall is 0.48-0.52. A third mode, A.A., gives 1.00/0.61 against 1.00/0.66. A.W. precision is depressed by the chain-counting rule.

checks.claim: Jelly approximate interpretation: recall 75.9%->88.1%, precision -1.5%, +55.1% edges, 9 OOM, time <10% for 76/141, >2x for 20
checks.corrected: The benchmarks are 141 Node.js programs (71 npm packages, 70 GitHub projects), 36 of them with dynamic call graphs. TypeScript is handled by ignoring annotations. No React, JSX or React Native code is evaluated. The -12.3 figure is one project's precision drop.
checks.source: Laursen, Xu, Moller PLDI 2024, cs.au.dk PDF text

checks.claim: Legunsen: class-level static RTS unsafe 0.2%, imprecise 33.0%; method-level 10.6%, 55.7%; method level slower than RetestAll
checks.corrected: The numbers are right, but they are the percentage of revisions with any violation against Ekstazi, not the share of tests missed. Data: 985 revisions of 22 Java projects; 2 projects (class level) against 14 (method level) had safety violations. The paper also advises plain RetestAll for suites running under about 5 s.
checks.source: Legunsen et al. FSE 2016 PDF, section 4.2

checks.claim: FastAPI app.openapi() is public, builds the schema from app.routes, and is callable without a server
checks.corrected: The docs confirm the public .openapi() method, the get_openapi call over app.routes and the openapi_schema cache. They never state that it runs without a server; that follows from the code, not the docs.

checks.claim: APIRoute carries dependant, response_model, endpoint, dependencies, operation_id (semi-private, pin version)
checks.corrected: At master, __init__ assigns only self.app; the other attributes are set through the _populate_api_route_state helper, so the internals are being refactored. The repo allows fastapi>=0.115,<1.0, which is unpinned.

checks.claim: CodeQL is excluded for a private repo by its licence
checks.corrected: Use with a non-open-source codebase requires a paid GitHub Advanced Security licence.

checks.claim: SCIP is a transmission format, not a storage or query format
scip-python and scip-typescript are real, maintained and usable offline in a Linux container
checks.corrected: scip-python 0.6.8 (2026-10-22): MIT (Pyright's licence text), 20.3 MB unpacked, Node 16+, Python 3.10+ only, and --environment JSON to skip pip. scip-typescript 0.6.2 (2026-11-10): Apache-2.0, requires Node >=22.23.4, and bundles TypeScript ^6.0.3 while the repo uses 5.3.3. Use --infer-tsconfig for plain JavaScript.
checks.source: registry.npmjs.org metadata; scip-python LICENSE.txt and README; scip-typescript README

checks.claim: sys.monitoring (3.12) offers PY_START/PY_RETURN/CALL with per-location DISABLE; coverage.py dynamic_context=test_function records per-test lines into SQLite
checks.corrected: The mechanisms are confirmed, but no overhead figure exists in the docs. Coverage contexts record lines per test, not call edges, so a line-to-definition join is needed. coverage.py is not a backend dependency, so using it is an install.

checks.claim: dmypy inspect --show definition is documented and experimental
checks.corrected: Only --show definition is marked experimental. It needs a completed dmypy check, and --export-types is recommended. mypy is unpinned (>=1.13,<3.0).

checks.claim: ARISE: SWE-agent with Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, 22.0% (+4.7 points), Recall@1 0.43->0.60, no token figures
checks.corrected: Abstract only: 66 of 300 tasks, one backbone. Weak evidence.

checks.claim: v1 has 77 backend routes, the repo has 63 response_model uses, and the web app is 120 JS files with no TypeScript
checks.corrected: 77 backend routes plus 8 ops routes (85 route nodes). At HEAD: 63 response_model= uses, 78 route decorators, 120 .js/.jsx files and 0 .ts/.tsx.
checks.source: local re-count: frozen-commit nodes.jsonl, git grep, git ls-files

checks.claim: v1's test-to-code evidence is 39 test_calls_route edges
checks.corrected: The frozen commit has 441 test_calls_route records: 382 distinct pairs from 274 test functions to 83 routes.

checks.claim: Uschold and Gruninger: stratified CQs; all-lookup CQs is not a well-designed ontology; designs answering the same CQ are equivalent and 'any comparison must use other criteria'
checks.corrected: These are method statements; the paper carries no outcome evidence.

checks.claim: Zhou, Huang, Scholkopf 2006: clique subedges weighted w(e)/delta(e); random walk picks a hyperedge by weight, then a vertex uniformly
ROSE ignores changes over 30 entities; predicts 26% of further files and 15% of functions; top three correct 64%
checks.corrected: The 30-entity cap was introduced to skip CVS branch-merge transactions, not as a sweep-noise rule. 15% and 26% are entity-level recall and precision. At file level, given one file, ROSE predicts 26% of the co-changed files and the top three hold a correct file in 70% of transactions; 64% is the entity-level figure. Data: 8 CVS projects, 10,761 transactions.
checks.source: Zimmermann et al. ICSE 2004 PDF text

checks.claim: HistoryFinder table (CodeShovel 93.44/84.17/88.56 ... GitFuncName 41.33/68.99/51.69); independent re-evaluation
checks.corrected: The numbers are exact but come from the HistoryFinder oracle, built by the HistoryFinder authors: independent for the other tools, self-evaluated for HistoryFinder. On the corrected CodeShovel oracle, CodeShovel's F1 is about 96-97. The oracle is 200 Java methods. HistoryFinder's body-similarity thresholds are 70% within a file and 75% across files.

checks.claim: CodexGraph: 22.16k vs 1.47k tokens (BM25) on CrossCodeEval Lite and 102.25k vs 14.76k on SWE-bench Lite; EM 27.90 vs 21.20; tied with AutoCodeRover at 22.96; schema empirically designed, no ablation
checks.corrected: GPT-4o backbone; token costs are reported for GPT-4o only.

checks.claim: Knowledge Vault: extractor scores are not on one scale; Platt scaling; 0.9 predicted is about 90% true; 1.6B triples
checks.source: Dong et al. KDD 2014 PDF, section 3.3

checks.claim: Gao et al. 2019: entity-clustered sampling, cost c1 per entity plus c2 per triple, up to 60% (static) and 80% (evolving) cost reduction
checks.corrected: Measured c1 was 45 s per entity on their annotation task. The savings are at web-scale KGs and are small at a few hundred labels.

checks.claim: Fatemi et al. 2020: 61% of Freebase relations are non-binary; star-to-clique loses information
checks.corrected: Both statements are in the body, not the abstract. The evidence is link prediction, not retrieval.

checks.claim: StarE: 17.4% of 734M Wikidata statements carry qualifiers; up to 25 MRR points
checks.corrected: 128M of 734M statements (August 2019). The 25 MRR points are on link prediction only.

checks.claim: Dagenais and Robillard 2012: doc-to-code links with 96% average precision and recall on four systems
checks.corrected: Confirmed at abstract level only (the PDF host returned 403); the systems are Java.

checks.claim: v1 counts: 36 edge kinds, 177 usable commits (median 7 files), 16-30-file commits give 55% of 8,411 pair incidences, 930 of 1,896 co_changed edges rest only on commits of 10+ files, calls confidence 4,176/599/111
checks.corrected: Reproduced exactly. Note that the task brief's '37 edge kinds' is wrong: there are 36.
checks.source: local re-count (scratchpad va/chk.js) of frozen-commit facts

checks.claim: v1 section, URL-site and invariant ids embed line numbers or ordinals
checks.corrected: inv:CLAUDE.md#<ordinal>, 452 sec:...#L<line> ids, 122 urlsite:<path>:<line>:... ids, and 580 of 5,464 node ids carrying a line number. The lane's churn and survival percentages were not re-derived.

checks.claim: Pruned landmark labelling: the smallest evaluated graph has 63k nodes
checks.corrected: Gnutella, 63K nodes and 148K edges. The timing table was not re-checked.
checks.source: Akiba et al. SIGMOD 2013, arXiv 1304.4661 PDF

checks.claim: GRAIL authors call DFS attractive on small graphs
checks.corrected: Stronger than stated: their 'small' datasets have 3,617-38,811 nodes (sparse) and 6,000-10,720 (dense), the same order as this graph.

checks.claim: Hohenstein and Jergler: 500k nodes, 5-hop query 59.7 s warm without an index and 4.5 s with one; cited MySQL about 6x faster than Neo4j at 5 hops
checks.corrected: PostgreSQL, Table 1: 59.67 s against 4.54 s. The 6x figure is from Baach 2015 as cited.

checks.claim: Faldu et al.: 16.8% average speed-up; reordering can destroy community structure; 18M-64M vertices; 25 MB cache
checks.corrected: The abstract confirms 16.8% (against 11.6% for the best prior technique, 40 application-dataset pairs) and says reordering 'may' destroy community structure. Graph sizes and cache size were not verified (body not opened).

checks.claim: WebGraph: 3.08 bits per link on 118M pages and 1B links
Hanauer et al.: dynamic reachability algorithms beat static and caching BFS/DFS
checks.corrected: The setting is single-edge update streams interleaved with queries, which does not match per-commit batch changes with a 25 ms rebuild. The lane's conclusion holds for scale reasons, not on this paper's support.
checks.source: Hanauer, Henzinger, Schulz ALENEX 2020 PDF conclusion

checks.claim: Glean: one ownership unit per file is recommended; a derived fact is visible only if all its sources are
checks.corrected: No timings given; propagation is O(facts).

checks.claim: Graph text encoding changes LLM accuracy by 4.8-61.8%
checks.corrected: The range is the boost from choosing the right encoder on synthetic graph-reasoning tasks (GraphQA). It is not evidence about compressing identifiers in code-retrieval answers.

checks.claim: Graph size: 5,460 nodes and 17,370 distinct typed edges (audit 5,464 and 16,462)
checks.corrected: Frozen commit: 5,464 nodes, 18,875 edge records, 17,410 distinct (src, dst, kind), 36 kinds. The task brief says 16,500 and 37; modelling says 18,900. Reconcile on one definition.

checks.claim: Engine fallbacks: LadybugDB MIT 5.8 MB wheel; DuckDB 2.0 + DuckPGQ (15.4 MB) offline in a Linux container
checks.corrected: DuckDB 2.0.0 (MIT) exists. DuckPGQ installs FROM community over the network, so it must be vendored for offline use, and DuckDB 2.0 needs SET active_grammar_extensions. LadybugDB is on PyPI as 'ladybug' 0.22.3 (MIT, Python 3.10-3.14); the 5.8 MB wheel size is unverified (the 0.16.0 cp312 wheel was 7.7 MB).
checks.source: duckdb.org community extension page; pypi.org JSON for duckdb and ladybug

recommendations_to_drop_or_weaken: Construction 'dynamic test-run edges': weaken from 'do after measurement' to a trial that must beat a file-level static baseline. Legunsen found class-level static selection unsafe in only 0.2% of revisions against dynamic Ekstazi, and advises running all tests for suites under about 5 s. v1 already has 441 test-to-route records, not 39. Coverage contexts give lines, not calls, and coverage.py is an install.

Construction 'three-tier field-level contract edges': weaken from 'do' to 'trial'. Tiers 1-2 stand on strong mechanisms (OpenAPI export, TypeScript checker). Tier 3, a home-made def-use pass over untyped JavaScript, rests only on ARISE's abstract (one backbone, no token data); build it last, gated by its 'beats co-change only' test.

Modelling R3 (hyperedge change sets weighted w/|e|): keep it as cheap, but drop the 'moderate recall gain' expectation. The mathematics is confirmed, but ROSE's 30-entity cap was a CVS branch-merge filter, not evidence about sweep noise, and v1 already ties a plain co-change list. Expect value for 'and why' questions (message, PR), not for ranking.

Modelling R4 identity ladder: keep, but start the body-similarity threshold sweep at 0.70-0.75 (HistoryFinder's values), not 0.8. Do not quote the Java tool accuracies as an expectation: HistoryFinder's own numbers are self-evaluated on its authors' oracle.

Modelling R2 (metapath discovery from example pairs): weaken to 'only if the competency-question schema check (R1) leaves a gap'. Its sources were read as summaries only, the evidence comes from biology and bibliographic networks, and 65 tuning commits invite overfitting.

Modelling R6 (calibrated confidence): keep the field split as hygiene and drop any expected ranking gain. Knowledge Vault calibrated at 1.6B triples; here the parser-exact kinds are already about 1.0.
Storage 'typed arrays in process': optional and justified by simplicity only. Milliseconds against a model step of seconds give no agent-visible gain.

Storage 'containment-aware answer format': keep as a trial, but drop the 4.8-61.8% citation as support (synthetic graph-reasoning tasks, not identifier compression). Token savings stay estimates until a real tokenizer counts them.

Any graph tool arm: take CodexGraph (7-15x BM25 tokens for equal or slightly better results) as the default expectation, and require every arm to beat a plain-search baseline on tokens, not only on recall.

Keep as rejections, now on verified grounds: Jelly (no React or React Native evaluation), CodeQL (licence), and reachability indexes, reordering and compression (GRAIL's own 'small' datasets are this graph's size).
feasibility_problems: FastAPI APIRoute internals are being refactored at master (attributes now set through _populate_api_route_state), and the backend allows fastapi>=0.115,<1.0. A route-table walk must pin the exact FastAPI version of the Docker image, or use only the public app.openapi().

Importing the FastAPI app without a database looks feasible: Settings() has defaults and create_async_engine does not connect at import. It still needs the full backend dependency set, so run it in the project image. Other import side effects (for example Sentry init) were not checked.

scip-typescript 0.6.2 requires Node >=22.23.4 and bundles TypeScript ^6.0.3, while the mobile app pins ~5.3.3. Disagreements with v1 may come from the compiler version. The web app needs --infer-tsconfig.
scip-python needs an --environment JSON to avoid calling pip offline. It is 20.3 MB unpacked before dependencies and supports Python 3.10+ only.

coverage.py (and pytest-cov) is not a backend dependency, so per-test contexts are an install for the owner to decide. A hand-written sys.monitoring collector has no documented overhead figure. Integration tests need Postgres (the Docker gate provides it).
mypy's build.build is an internal API, dmypy inspect --show definition is experimental, and mypy is unpinned (>=1.13,<3.0).

DuckPGQ installs from the DuckDB community repository over the network and must be vendored for an offline container; DuckDB 2.0 also needs SET active_grammar_extensions. This only matters if the engine verdict is reopened.
No offline tokenizer exists, so every token figure in the storage lane is a character-based estimate.

Counts drift across documents: 36 edge kinds, not 37; 18,875 edge records and 17,410 distinct typed edges, against 16,462, 16,500, 17,370 and 18,900 cited elsewhere; 441 test-to-route records, not 39. The design must state one definition.

b.summary:
I re-checked 42 claims across the three lanes against their primary sources: 33 confirmed, 9 partly, none unsupported. I also re-ran the ranking pilot read-only from its cached feature files.

**The pilot reproduces.**
- On the 50 late tuning commits, rank fusion of PageRank and co-change (RRF) beats PageRank alone by +0.027 to +0.030 P@10 for fusion constants 10, 30, 60 and 120. Every interval is above zero.
- The 25-feature and 2-feature models stay within -0.003 to +0.002 of each other across ridge penalties 0.3, 3, 30 and 300, so the lane's choice of penalty favoured nothing.
- Tie noise from random ordering is about 0.004 P@10.

**Corrections that matter for the design:**
- **EdgeBank:** under historical negatives it is best only on UN Trade. CAWN wins UN Vote (0.75 vs 0.71) and Contact (0.80 vs 0.77); the paper's own text over-claims.
- **Recurrency baseline:** it is 9th to 10th on ICEWS14 and ICEWS18. It ranks first or third only on recurrence-heavy sets.
- **SEAL:** the Power comparison used SimRank (76.15) as the reference, but the ensemble heuristic scores 79.52.
- **Adaptive-k:** it does not match fixed top-k in its own GPT-4o factoid table (73.33 vs 76.33 to 78.00). This weakens the published support for the proposed stop rule.
- **LocAgent:** its ablation (search entry point worth 19 points, traversal about 2) is a fine-tuned 7B model on an unnamed dataset.
- **Legunsen:** the 0.2 % and 10.6 % figures are shares of revisions with any safety violation relative to dynamic test selection, not shares of tests missed.
- **Build Systems à la Carte:** the paper supports the premise-ledger design but not the wording "early cutoff on prose is unsound". The unsound case is a deep trace over a non-deterministic task; early cutoff on such a task just fails to fire.
- **History-length study (Moonen et al.):** the 25,000-commit figure and the 8-file transaction cap are unverified today. Both Simula PDFs are behind a bot check.

**Confirmed tool status:**
- DDlog was archived on 13 July 2026.
- Feldera is MIT-licensed, ships a Docker image, and needs about 13 GB to build from source.
- Souffle is UPL-licensed with provenance support and no incremental mode.
- PyKEEN 1.11.1 dates from April 2025 and supports Python 3.12.
- pcst_fast has no ARM Linux wheel.
- leidenalg 0.12.0 ships abi3 wheels and needs igraph installed separately.
- AnyBURL's latest release is BSD-3 (bug fix 12.11.2025); the Java version it needs is not stated.

Full notes are in the notes file.

checks.claim: Proximity predictors beat random by 40-50x; Katz variants often best; best predictor ~16% correct; STOC/FOCS <= ~7x
checks.corrected: Katz variant best on 3 of 5 arXiv sections; random predictor correct 0.15-0.48%; train 1994-96 test 1997-99.

checks.claim: RA marginally best: USAir RA 0.955 vs AA 0.925; PB 0.931 vs 0.922
checks.corrected: CN (0.937) also beats AA on USAir; random 90/10 split, 10 repeats, random negatives.

checks.claim: SEAL beat best heuristic on 7 of 8 graphs; Power 76.15 to 87.61
checks.corrected: 7 of 8 vs heuristics is right (6 of 8 vs all baselines). On Power the best heuristic is ENS 79.52; 76.15 is SimRank. Gap 8.1 points, not 11.5. 90% of edges are positives, negatives random.

checks.claim: HeaRT: collab Katz 6.31/RA 6.29 vs GCN 6.09/SAGE 5.53; ppa RA 28.34 vs SAGE 27.27; Cora GAE 18.32 vs AA 11.91; Pubmed SAGE 9.40 vs Katz 3.01
checks.corrected: 'Same tuning budget' is not stated as such; the paper keeps the training process and parameter ranges the same as the existing setting.

checks.claim: SFE matches PRA (MAP .344 vs .337 Freebase, .319 vs .303 NELL); 44 min vs 5 min; abstract .432 to .528
checks.source: Gardner and Mitchell EMNLP 2015, aclanthology D15-1173 (pdftotext)

checks.claim: AnyBURL H@1 FB15k-237 27.34 vs RotatE 23.83; WN18RR 45.69 vs 42.60; pc=5; Rossi: only ComplEx-N3 comparable
checks.corrected: Baselines are copied from Rossi et al.; AnyBURL release 23-1x got a bug fix on 12.11.2025, BSD-3; required Java version not stated.

design.summary:
DESIGN.md (283 lines) derives graph v2 from the measured competency questions and the documented theory. v2 is a typed property graph used as a knowledge graph in Hogan's sense: a schema derived from competency questions (CQs), stable identity, provenance and a per-build quality card. It adds a temporal layer (validity sets over the commit graph, with premises re-checked on change) and n-ary nodes for change sets, rules with roles, and claims with premise sets. It is not a forecasting TKG, not an embedding model and not a GNN, and the reasons are given with numbers. Model-written content enters only as ledger claims with recorded premises, never as code edges.

Each component states: the theory and its sources, what it replaces in v1, the alternatives rejected, the expected effect, a tuning-data ablation with a stated cut rule, its build cost, its installs and its tier.

The ceiling is stated from the owner's own records. The CQs a graph can serve carry 38 % of product carried tokens (about 8.8 % of product context) and about 21 % of program context. My illustration, not a forecast: with answers one fifth the size of the reads they replace, and half adoption, v2 could move about 3-5 % of product context and about 8 % of program context. It could also cost tokens: CodexGraph used 7-15x the tokens of BM25. Only an agent pilot can show the real share.

Corrections applied from the verifiers:
- 36 edge kinds, 18,875 edge records and 17,410 distinct edges.
- 441 test-to-route records, not 39.
- The ROSE 30-entity cap was a CVS branch-merge filter, not a noise rule.
- The stop rule is demoted to a trial (Adaptive-k scored 73.33 against 76.33-78.00 for fixed budgets).
- Dynamic test edges are demoted to a trial.
- The Moonen et al. figures (8-file cap, 25,000 commits) are unverified and not used.

I built and ran nothing in this lane; the numbers come from the lane notes and verifier notes.

design.agent_tool:
One command-line program called through Bash, so no schema sits in the prefix; a pushed pointer of at most 500 tokens stays stable across commits. Operations:
- find <words>: exact name, then BM25; at most 8 lines.
- around <entity> --intent uses|impact|contract|tests|rules|history: 1,000 tokens by default, 2,000 hard cap.
- rules <path|symbol|diff>: constraining rules with role, source line and status.
- brief <phase|slice>: the phase's sections, its items with their defining blocks, the rules on its area and the slice card, under a budget.
- connect <a> <b> ...: an exact Steiner tree, at most 12 lines.
- since <commit> [anchors]: the changes near the anchors since that commit.
- notes <entity> and record ...: only with the ledger.

Output is a file-grouped tree carrying path:line evidence and relation tags, with a footer naming what was omitted by kind and slice, and explicit unknown or unanchored markers. Sources: LocAgent, the SWE-agent ACI study, the small-agent caps study and Anthropic's tool guidance. A query-language tool and paging are rejected (CypherBench, CodexGraph, SWE-agent).
validation_plan: Tuning data only: 65 tuning commits (388 T1 seeds, leak-free parent builds), the 191 cached snapshots, tuning typed questions extended to 40-60 hand-verified questions with truth read from code, and recorded transcripts for the brief and ledger replays (13 product sessions from one day: descriptive weight only)
Rolling-origin splits (train on at least 15 earlier commits, score the late 50); an inner rolling split for every parameter; no random splits
Paired bootstrap clustered by commit; arms declared in advance; random tie-breaking with the tie share reported; a placebo feature; a learning curve; the one-standard-error simplicity rule
Resolution is about 0.02 P@10 and 0.065 recall (paired SD 0.263); a component whose gain is below that is cut in favour of the simpler form

Zero-model tests run first: CQ forward and backward checks, the identity replay (zero mis-binding), the mutation test (zero stale), the ledger replay, the K1 diff, the field-contract test, ranker and selection curves, and tool output sizes
The 75 held-out commits are spent: one declared run of the final configuration, reported as descriptive only. Commits after the frozen commit are few: descriptive only

Agent pilot as the decisive test (owner decision): arms are no tool, the v2 tool, a BM25-only index, a placebo tool and graphify as shipped. Outcome: total tokens for the same correct work, with adoption, steps and stale serves logged. Every graph arm must beat plain search on tokens

2. M6 stable identity and T1 validity sets (the precondition for anything stored)
3. M3 + K5 meaning layer, the brief and rules operations, T5 citation facts (the largest measured cost: CQ2, CQ4 and the session start)
4. K1 framework export, M2 + K4 tiers 1-2, M1 additions (literals, members, reads_column)

refute.verdict:
The design is a real improvement on v1, but its claim that every choice comes from documented theory does not hold yet. It starts from the measured questions, names its sources, carries the verifiers' corrections and keeps the agent pilot as the only test of tokens. Four problems remain.

1. Improvised choices and miscited sources remain:
   - About a dozen thresholds have no source.
   - The M3 role vocabulary is hand-made.
   - S2's stop rule uses the wrong value for F: 695 tokens is what a scripted search read per typed question. Counting the carry over the remaining calls, an avoided search is worth about 13,000 tokens.
   - Three sources are cited for things they do not say:
     - Hogan's knowledge-graph definition is inclusive, so v1 was already a knowledge graph.
     - The in-lists and out-lists cited to de Kleer belong to Doyle's JTMS.
     - S2's "own derivation" is in fact the marginal value theorem and the information patch model.
2. The validation plan drops the use-case lane's own test set: CQ instances taken from transcripts and weighted by carried tokens. So the zero-model evidence again scores co-change truth and hand-written typed questions, not the measured use. The whole ranking stack serves a question that is not among the 16 recorded CQs.
3. Several tuning tests cannot fail, or are biased:
   - The M1 coverage check and the M6 "cut by about a third" rule pass by construction.
   - The Q1 prune test leans toward cutting kinds.
   - The M3 replay leans toward passing.
   - The A1 brief test passes on file names alone.
   - T4 has no threshold.
   - K1, S1, R4 and R5 have no cut rule.
   - R1 re-runs the pilot on the same 65 commits, without the scripted-search arm an agent actually uses.
   - No clean confirmation set remains: the 75 held-out commits are spent, and only 16 commits (10 touching product code) exist after the frozen commit.
4. The decisive agent pilot, as round 2 sized it (about 40 tasks), detects only savings of about 20 to 25 %. The design's own illustration is 3 to 5 % of product context.

Leak paths the design does not close:
- Hand-assigned invariant roles taken from today's CLAUDE.md text, which names later migrations and PRs.
- Held-out-period snapshots inside the "tuning data".
- In-sample transcript replays: the same 13 sessions produced the question list and would score the brief.

Most program documents are off the commit history: 1,780 untracked files against 124 tracked. So T1/T4 cannot cover most of the 1,147M program carried tokens, and CQ1 conclusions mostly rest on unverifiable premises such as papers, web pages and scratch measurements.

Components that hold up: the storage choice, the not-worth-it list, A1's no-query-language/no-paging stance, K1/K2/K5/K6, T2/T5 and the R1 measurement itself.

claims.claim: v2 is a knowledge graph in Hogan's sense because it has a schema, stable identity, provenance and quality measures
claims.detail: Hogan et al. 2021 (introduction, PDF text extracted) use an inclusive definition: a graph of data meant to accumulate and convey knowledge, with entity nodes and relation edges. Schema, identity, context and quality are aspects the survey discusses, not requirements. By that definition v1 was already a knowledge graph; v2 adds the aspects.

claims.claim: v2 is not a temporal knowledge graph
claims.detail: It is a TKG in the representation sense (facts with validity over a branching commit history). It is not a TKG in the forecasting or completion sense (TLogic, RE-Net). Neither research round reviewed the representation-sense TKG literature.

claims.claim: The CQs a graph can serve carry 38% of product carried tokens (8.8% of product context) and about 21% of program context
claims.detail: The arithmetic checks (91.9M of 242M). The program figure leans on CQ1 (521M), which has the noisiest label, and its conclusions mostly rest on papers, web pages and scratch measurements that T4 cannot check.

claims.claim: Illustration: v2 could move about 3-5% of product context and about 8% of program context
claims.detail: Correctly labelled as an illustration. It must never be stated as a forecast, and it is far below what the planned pilot can detect: round 2's power script needs about a 20-25% per-task saving for 80% power at about 40 tasks.

claims.claim: CodexGraph used 7-15x the tokens of BM25 for equal or slightly better results
claims.detail: Confirmed by verify-a (M5). One system, GPT-4o only.

claims.claim: Q1: store the CQ registry as data, with forward and backward checks
claims.detail: The registry is sound. The kind-prune test (recall must fall beyond the paired 95% interval on T1 plus 20 typed questions) cannot show the value of a kind that serves a CQ with only 1-2 questions, so it prunes by absence of evidence. Decide kinds by per-CQ answerability instead.

claims.claim: M1 closes the 11.2% definition gap (from 88.8% to over 97%)
claims.detail: The test cannot fail: adding nodes for variables and members raises coverage by construction. 88.8% is the held-out figure; the tuning baseline is 91.3% (364 of 4,162 missing).

claims.claim: M1: drop references_literal if under a third of recorded usage searches target a literal
claims.detail: The threshold has no source. CQ8 in total is 4.2% of product carried tokens.

claims.claim: M2/K4 tiers 1-2 give exact field contracts
claims.detail: Run them as a trial behind the K4 test. CQ13 is only 1.0% of product carried tokens (2.4M) and 2.9M of program.

claims.claim: K4 tier 3: a def-use pass over untyped web JavaScript
claims.detail: It rests on one abstract (ARISE: one backbone, weak) and costs days for under 1% of carried tokens. Not worth building.

claims.claim: M3 meaning layer is the largest candidate saving
claims.detail: It is the largest addressable cost (CQ2 plus CQ4: 17% of product, 22% of program), not a saving. The 55% session-start share includes code orientation, so it is not M3's share. Most of that cost can be reached by an outline-and-ID index or by orchestrator-written briefs, with no relations.

claims.claim: M3 constrains edges carry theory-derived roles (guard, client half, condition input, example, violation)
claims.detail: The W3C n-ary note justifies making a rule a node. It says nothing about which roles; the role vocabulary is hand-made.

claims.claim: M3 tuning test (ii): if sections later cited or acted on exceed half of what was read, demote the layer
claims.detail: Use is measured from transcripts where only 9% of model calls carry visible text. Use is under-observed, so the test leans toward passing.

claims.claim: M4 ledger: no stale conclusion is served
claims.detail: This holds only for conclusions whose premises are in the repository, and 'stale' is judged against the extractor's facts. How often conclusions are reused is unmeasured, and the nearby evidence is flat to negative.

claims.claim: M4 theory: justifications with in-lists and out-lists [deKleer]

claims.detail: Its cut condition (cut spurious invalidations by about a third) re-measures a known 34% (736 of 2,179 vanished ids are line-number moves). Its value depends on M4 conclusions being reused, which is untested.

claims.claim: M7 splits evidence and confidence per method class

claims.detail: CypherBench best 61.58%; iterative paging scored 12.0% against 15.7% with no search tool.

claims.claim: A1 caps: 1,000 tokens by default, 2,000 hard
claims.detail: The cited caps come from a study of models up to 32B. They are untested for frontier agents.

claims.detail: A list of names passes it while saving nothing. Score the content the agent would still have to read, and add the strongest simple arms: heading and ID extraction, and an orchestrator-written brief.

claims.claim: A2: tree format is 0.43x the tokens of triples
claims.detail: For size only. The accuracy evidence is about one sample out of 37.

claims.claim: A3: pointer of at most 500 tokens, about 0.35% of tokens
claims.detail: Adoption needs steering beyond a pointer: in CodeCompass, 58% of graph-condition trials made no graph call.

claims.claim: ST1: SQLite plus in-process arrays; no graph database
claims.detail: At this size. Revisit at about 10^5 nodes.

claims.claim: Section 9: not worth it at this size
claims.detail: GRAIL's own small sets (3.6k-39k nodes) support it.

claims.claim: Validation plan: rolling origin, paired bootstrap, declared arms, one-standard-error rule
claims.detail: It drops the transcript-derived, carried-token-weighted CQ test set. No clean confirmation set remains. Document facts must be taken as of each commit.

claims.claim: The held-out commits are spent; one run is reported as descriptive only
claims.detail: Only 16 commits (10 touching product code) exist after the frozen commit a31924a (2026-08-03).

claims.claim: The agent pilot is the decisive test
claims.detail: At about 40 tasks it has 0.02-0.09 power at a true 10% saving. It cannot see the design's own 3-5% illustration. Focus the pilot on tasks the served CQs dominate, or add a lookup-level replay.

claims.claim: The owner-words table covers every phrase honestly
claims.detail:
These need plain wording:
- 'Semantic relations': v2 has no meaning-similarity retrieval.
- 'Spatial topology': it is only the folder tree and the slice quotient.
- 'Temporal': mostly harness infrastructure.
- 'Knowledge graph' and 'TKG': need the Hogan and two-sense corrections.

claims.claim: 12b: earlier rounds never treated ranking as link prediction, selection as knapsack, identity or n-ary modelling
claims.detail: But v2 repeats round 1's habit of validating mainly on co-change truth.
